questions.rationale: Accuracy, stability, plain copper cable and simpler calibration. Withstanding 1200 degC is a thermocouple advantage, not an RTD one.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: For a ferro alloy furnace shell temperature at around 1400 degC, the correct choice is:

options.B: A high-temperature thermocouple such as Type R, S or B

questions.rationale: Well beyond RTD range. The noble metal types are made for exactly this duty.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: For a cold storage application at minus 40 degC, a suitable choice would be:

options.B: Pt100 RTD or Type T thermocouple

questions.rationale: RTDs work well down to about minus 200 degC, and Type T is designed for low temperature. Types B, R and S are high temperature devices with poor low-end output.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A thermocouple loop reads correctly at ambient but drifts increasingly as the process heats. The most likely cause is:

options.B: A wrong extension cable or an unintended junction in the wiring

questions.rationale: Error that grows with temperature difference points at a mismatched extension cable creating a parasitic junction.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Which technology allows the transmitter to be mounted remotely from the sensor with least error?

options.B: RTD in three or four-wire configuration, using ordinary copper cable
options.E: Neither, both must be head mounted

questions.rationale: Three and four-wire RTD configurations compensate the lead resistance, and the cable is ordinary copper. Thermocouples require matching extension cable throughout.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A client specifies a thermocouple where our review shows an RTD would be more accurate and cheaper to wire. The correct action is:

options.B: Quote as specified and raise the observation as a technical query with the reasoning
options.E: Quote the RTD and explain at site

questions.rationale: Quote to specification, raise the query with reasoning. Silent substitution creates a deviation nobody approved.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: DP level measurement infers level from:

options.A: The dielectric constant of the fluid
options.B: The hydrostatic head, which is the pressure exerted by the column of liquid
options.C: The time of flight of a pulse

questions.rationale: Hydrostatic head. The transmitter measures pressure and the level is calculated from it, which is why density matters.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: The hydrostatic pressure at the base of a liquid column depends on:

options.B: Height, density and gravitational acceleration

questions.rationale: P equals rho g h. The tank diameter is irrelevant, which surprises people the first time they meet it.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Water of density 1000 kg per cubic metre stands 2 metres deep. Taking g as 9.81, what is the hydrostatic pressure at the base, in kPa? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: 1000 x 9.81 x 2 equals 19620 Pa, or 19.62 kPa.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: If the density of the liquid in a tank falls but the DP transmitter is not recalibrated, the indicated level will be:

options.B: Lower than actual

questions.rationale: Less dense liquid produces less head for the same height, so the transmitter reads low. Density change is the fundamental weakness of DP level.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A wet leg is used on a closed tank when:

options.A: The tank is at atmospheric pressure
options.B: The vapour in the tank condenses and would otherwise partially fill the impulse line unpredictably

questions.rationale: A deliberately filled reference leg gives a known, stable head rather than an unpredictable partial condensate column.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A dry leg reference connection is suitable when:

options.B: The vapour space stays dry and will not condense in the impulse line
options.C: The tank is open to atmosphere

questions.rationale: Dry legs only work if nothing condenses. If it does, the leg fills unpredictably and the reading wanders.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Zero suppression is required when:

options.A: The transmitter is above the lower tapping
options.B: The transmitter is mounted below the lower tapping, so a permanent head is present at zero level

questions.rationale: Mounting below the tapping means the transmitter always sees some head. Suppression shifts the calibrated zero to compensate.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Zero elevation is required when:

options.A: A wet leg produces a permanent negative differential at zero level
options.B: The tank is taller than 10 m
options.D: The transmitter is mounted at the tapping

questions.rationale: A filled wet leg produces a negative differential at zero level, so the calibrated zero must be elevated to suit.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Point level measurement differs from continuous measurement in that point devices:

options.B: Detect only whether the level is above or below a fixed position

questions.rationale: Point devices give a switch output at one position. They are common for high and low alarms and for overfill protection.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Select all continuous level measurement technologies.

options.B: Radar

questions.rationale: DP, radar, ultrasonic and capacitance are continuous. A vibrating fork is a point switch.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: On a boiler drum, DP level measurement is complicated by:

options.B: The density of both the water and the steam varying strongly with pressure

questions.rationale: Water and steam density both change with drum pressure, so an uncompensated DP reading is wrong at any pressure other than the calibration point. Pressure compensation is standard on boiler drum level.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: In a two-wire 4-20 mA loop, the components are connected:

options.B: In series - supply, transmitter and receiver all in one current path
options.C: In a star from the marshalling panel
options.E: With separate returns for each device

questions.rationale: Everything is in series in a single current path. That is why an extra indicator adds burden and why breaking the loop anywhere kills the signal.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Adding a panel indicator to an existing 4-20 mA loop affects:

options.B: The total loop burden, and therefore the supply voltage available to the transmitter

questions.rationale: The indicator adds resistance. If the budget was already tight the transmitter can drop out at 20 mA, which produces a fault that only appears at high readings.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A loop reads correctly at low values but the reading saturates and misbehaves near 20 mA. The most likely cause is:

options.B: Insufficient supply voltage for the loop burden at full current

questions.rationale: At 20 mA the voltage drop across the burden is greatest. If the supply cannot cover it plus the transmitter minimum, the loop collapses at the top of range only.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Where in a 4-20 mA loop is the current the same?

options.B: At every point in the series loop
options.D: Only when the shield is earthed

questions.rationale: Series current is identical everywhere. This is what makes the standard immune to cable resistance.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A three-wire transmitter has:

options.B: A shared common between the power supply and the signal return

questions.rationale: Power positive, signal, and a common return. It is used where the device needs more power than a two-wire loop can provide but does not justify four wires.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Reversing the polarity of a two-wire transmitter's terminals normally results in:

options.B: No current flow, and the loop reads zero or open circuit

questions.rationale: Most two-wire transmitters are polarity sensitive and simply do not conduct. Many are protected against damage, but none will read.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Where should the cable shield of an instrument loop be earthed?

options.B: At one end only, normally the control system cabinet, with the field end insulated

questions.rationale: One end only for low-frequency analogue signals. Earthing both ends creates a ground loop whose circulating current appears as noise on the signal.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Why must a field-end shield be insulated rather than simply left unconnected?

options.B: So it cannot accidentally contact the enclosure and create an unintended second earth

questions.rationale: An unterminated shield touching a metal gland or housing creates the second earth you were trying to avoid, and the fault is intermittent.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Select all good practices for routing instrument signal cable.

options.A: Segregate from power and motor cables
options.B: Cross power cables at right angles where crossing is unavoidable
options.C: Maintain a minimum separation distance in shared trays
options.D: Run alongside VFD output cables to save tray space
options.E: Use continuous shield with a single earth point

questions.rationale: Segregation, right-angle crossings, separation and single-point earthing. VFD output cables are the worst possible neighbour for a signal cable.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A transmitter signal shows noise that appears only when a nearby motor runs. The most likely cause is:

options.B: Electromagnetic coupling into the signal cable, usually from inadequate segregation or a shield fault

questions.rationale: Noise correlated with a specific piece of equipment is coupling. Check segregation and the shield before condemning the instrument.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A signal isolator is used in a loop to:

options.B: Break the galvanic path between two parts of the loop, removing earth loops and protecting equipment

questions.rationale: Galvanic separation. It solves earth loop problems and lets one signal feed two systems with different earth references.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: To share one transmitter signal with both the DCS and a third-party package, the correct approach is:

options.B: Wire both receivers in series if the burden allows, or use a signal splitter or isolator
options.D: Wire the second receiver to the shield
options.E: Split the pair at the junction box

questions.rationale: Series if the loop budget allows, otherwise a splitter or isolator. Wiring receivers in parallel breaks the series current principle entirely.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Ferrules on instrument terminations are used to:

options.B: Give a reliable, identifiable, mechanically sound termination that resists strand spreading

questions.rationale: Reliable mechanical termination and clear identification. Loose terminations are the most common fault found on site after a FAT.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: During loop checking, a current source is injected at the field terminals and the DCS reads correctly at 4, 12 and 20 mA. This proves:

options.B: The wiring, the input card and the scaling are correct, but says nothing about the sensor or transmitter

questions.rationale: Injection tests everything downstream of the injection point. The sensor and transmitter still need their own check.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Why should loop check records show the actual readings rather than just a tick?

options.B: Because the recorded values are the evidence of as-found accuracy and are needed if a dispute arises later

questions.rationale: Numbers are evidence; ticks are assertions. When a reading is disputed months later, only recorded values settle it.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A globe valve is classified as:

options.B: A sliding stem valve

questions.rationale: The plug slides linearly on a stem. Butterfly, ball and eccentric plug valves are rotary.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Which valve type generally offers the best throttling control and the widest range of trim options?

options.B: Ball

questions.rationale: The globe valve is the throttling workhorse. Its trim can be changed to alter characteristic, capacity and noise behaviour.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A butterfly valve is typically chosen when:

options.A: Precise throttling of a small flow is required
options.B: Large line sizes and low pressure drop with low cost are required
options.C: Very high pressure drop must be taken
options.D: Tight shutoff at high pressure is essential

questions.rationale: Large sizes, low cost, low permanent pressure loss. Its control performance and shutoff are inferior to a globe valve.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A gate valve should not be used for throttling because:

options.B: It is designed for isolation and throttling causes seat damage and unstable flow

questions.rationale: Gate valves are on/off devices. Partially open they erode and give poor, unstable control.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: The inherent flow characteristic of a valve describes:

options.A: Flow versus travel with constant pressure drop across the valve
options.B: Flow versus travel in the installed system

questions.rationale: Inherent characteristic assumes constant differential pressure. The installed characteristic, which is what the loop actually sees, differs because system pressure drop changes with flow.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: An equal percentage characteristic means that equal increments of travel produce:

options.B: Equal percentage changes in the existing flow
options.C: Flow proportional to the square of travel

questions.rationale: Each increment changes flow by the same percentage of the current flow. The result is small changes when nearly closed and large changes when nearly open.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Equal percentage trim is usually preferred when:

options.A: The pressure drop across the valve is constant
options.B: A large proportion of the system pressure drop is taken elsewhere, so valve differential falls as flow rises
options.C: Flow must be linear with travel
options.D: The valve is used for on/off duty
options.E: The service is clean water at fixed pressure

questions.rationale: Its rising gain offsets the falling process gain, giving a roughly linear installed characteristic and a more constant loop gain.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Linear trim is usually preferred when:

options.B: The pressure drop across the valve stays nearly constant across the flow range

questions.rationale: Constant differential means the inherent and installed characteristics are similar, so linear trim gives linear installed behaviour.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A spring and diaphragm actuator provides fail-safe action because:

options.B: The spring drives the valve to its designed position when air pressure is lost

questions.rationale: Stored spring energy is what makes the valve fail predictably. A double-acting piston actuator without an accumulator or spring will fail in place.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A valve positioner is fitted to:

options.B: Compare the actual stem position with the demanded position and drive the actuator until they match

questions.rationale: Closed-loop position control at the valve. It overcomes friction, packing effects and actuator hysteresis that a plain I/P cannot.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: An I/P converter converts:

options.B: Pressure to current

questions.rationale: Current to pressure, typically 4-20 mA to 3-15 psi or 0.2-1.0 bar, to drive a pneumatic actuator.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Select all information needed from a datasheet before specifying a control valve.

options.A: Flow rate range and fluid properties
options.B: Inlet and outlet pressures at each flow condition
options.C: Required leakage class and fail action
options.E: The tag number of the associated transmitter

questions.rationale: Flow, pressures, leakage and fail action, line size and rating. The transmitter tag is documentation, not sizing data.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Rangeability, or turndown, of a control valve refers to:

options.B: The ratio of maximum to minimum controllable flow

questions.rationale: The ratio between maximum and minimum flow the valve can control. Below the minimum the valve is effectively on/off.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: An oversized control valve typically causes:

options.B: Poor control because it operates near the seat where its gain is high and its resolution is poor

questions.rationale: Operating at 5 to 10 percent travel means every small signal change produces a large flow change and the seat wears. Oversizing is the most common valve specification error.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A valve leakage class such as Class IV or Class VI describes:

options.A: The permissible external stem packing leak
options.B: The permissible seat leakage when the valve is fully closed

questions.rationale: Seat leakage when closed. Class VI is a soft-seat tight shutoff class; a control valve is not automatically an isolation valve.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Why is a two-wire RTD connection generally unsuitable for industrial measurement?

options.B: The lead resistance adds directly to the measured resistance and appears as a temperature error
options.D: It cannot be used above 100 degC

questions.rationale: The transmitter cannot distinguish lead resistance from element resistance, so every ohm of cable reads as extra temperature.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A three-wire RTD connection works by:

options.B: Using the third lead to measure and cancel the lead resistance, assuming all leads are equal

questions.rationale: It cancels lead resistance on the assumption the leads are matched. That assumption is why all three conductors must be the same type and length.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A four-wire RTD connection is the most accurate because:

options.B: Excitation current and measurement are on separate pairs, so lead resistance has no effect at all

questions.rationale: Separate current and sense pairs remove lead resistance completely rather than compensating for it. It is used for laboratory and reference accuracy.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Which RTD wiring configuration is the industrial default?

options.B: Three-wire

questions.rationale: Three-wire is the practical compromise - almost all the accuracy of four-wire with one fewer conductor.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: In a three-wire RTD installation, using different conductor lengths for the three leads will:

options.B: Break the compensation assumption and introduce an error

questions.rationale: Compensation assumes matched leads. Splicing one lead at a different point in a junction box is a real and easily missed error.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A head-mounted temperature transmitter is preferred over a direct RTD wiring run because:

options.B: The signal is converted to 4-20 mA at the sensor, so cable resistance and noise over the long run no longer affect the measurement
options.D: It provides cold junction compensation for RTDs

questions.rationale: Converting at the head means the long run carries a robust current signal rather than a millivolt or resistance signal.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Which thermocouple type has the highest output voltage per degree?

options.B: Type E

questions.rationale: Type E has the largest Seebeck coefficient of the common types, which makes it useful where signal-to-noise matters.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Which thermocouple type is best suited to cryogenic and low temperature service?

options.B: Type S

questions.rationale: Type T, copper-constantan, works well below zero. The noble metal types have very low output at low temperature.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Select all valid reasons to choose a Pt100 in three-wire configuration over a thermocouple for a reactor jacket temperature.

options.A: Better accuracy in the operating range
options.B: Ordinary copper cable can be used

questions.rationale: Accuracy, cable, stability and calibration. Higher maximum temperature is the thermocouple's advantage.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A thermocouple is wired with copper extension cable from the head to the marshalling panel. The consequence is:

options.A: No effect if the cable is shielded
options.B: A parasitic junction at the transition, producing an error that varies with the head temperature

questions.rationale: Two new junctions are created where copper meets the thermocouple alloys. The error tracks the temperature at that point, which is why the fault looks like drift.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A thermocouple reads high in summer and low in winter with a steady process. The most likely cause is:

options.B: A cold junction compensation error or an unintended junction at an ambient-exposed location

questions.rationale: An error that tracks ambient points straight at the cold junction or an unintended junction exposed to ambient.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Reversing the polarity of a thermocouple's connection produces:

options.B: A reading that moves in the wrong direction as process temperature changes

questions.rationale: The millivolt sign reverses, so the indicated temperature falls when the process rises. It is a classic reversed-pair symptom on a multipair cable.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: On a multipair instrument cable, thermocouple pairs must be:

options.B: Thermocouple extension pairs of the correct alloy, individually shielded where noise is a concern

questions.rationale: Alloy must match throughout. Individual pair shields prevent crosstalk between low-level millivolt signals.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Sensor break detection on a temperature transmitter drives the output:

options.B: To a configured upscale or downscale fault value, per NAMUR NE43

questions.rationale: Upscale or downscale to a NAMUR fault value. Which direction to choose is a safety decision - it must drive the process to its safe state.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: For a temperature input used in a trip function, sensor break should normally drive the output:

options.B: In the direction that causes the trip to act

questions.rationale: Whichever direction produces the safe state. On a high-temperature trip that is upscale; on a low-temperature trip it is downscale.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: The loop budget calculation determines:

options.B: Whether the supply voltage is sufficient for the transmitter's minimum operating voltage plus the drop across the total loop burden at 20 mA

questions.rationale: Supply voltage must cover the transmitter minimum plus burden times 20 mA. If it does not, the loop fails at the top of range.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A 24 V DC supply feeds a transmitter requiring a minimum of 12 V to operate. What is the maximum permissible total loop resistance, in ohms? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: (24 minus 12) divided by 0.020 equals 600 ohm. Anything above that and the transmitter drops out before reaching 20 mA.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A 24 V supply feeds a transmitter needing 14 V minimum. The loop contains a 250 ohm receiver and an isolator dropping 3 V. Ignoring cable, how many ohms of headroom remain for cable resistance? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: 24 minus 14 minus 3 leaves 7 V. 7 divided by 0.020 equals 350 ohm total; less the 250 ohm receiver leaves 100 ohm for cable.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: What voltage is developed across a 250 ohm receiver resistor at a loop current of 12 mA? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: 0.012 multiplied by 250 equals 3 V. At 4 mA it is 1 V and at 20 mA it is 5 V, giving the standard 1-5 V conversion.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Adding an intrinsic safety barrier to an existing loop affects the budget because:

options.B: It adds series resistance and an end-to-end voltage drop

questions.rationale: Barriers add resistance and drop voltage. Retrofitting one into a loop that had no headroom is a common cause of a loop that suddenly fails at high readings.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A loop worked correctly during FAT with a short bench cable but fails at 20 mA on site with a 700 m run. The cause is:

options.B: Cable resistance added to the burden, exceeding the loop budget

questions.rationale: Cable resistance was zero on the bench. This is exactly why the budget must be calculated using the site cable length, not the bench setup.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Increasing the supply voltage from 24 V to 30 V in a loop that was marginal will:

options.B: Increase the available headroom for burden, provided every device is rated for the higher voltage

questions.rationale: More headroom, but only if the transmitter, barrier and receiver are all rated for it. Check the ratings before changing the supply.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Select all contributors to total loop burden.

options.A: The receiver or input card resistance
options.B: The cable resistance, out and back

questions.rationale: Receiver, cable, barrier and any series device. The transmitter is the current source, not part of the burden it must drive.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Cable resistance in a loop budget must be counted:

options.B: For the full circuit, out and back

questions.rationale: Current travels out and returns, so both conductors count. Halving it is a common and expensive arithmetic error.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Using a larger conductor cross-section on a long instrument run:

options.B: Reduces cable resistance and therefore loop burden

questions.rationale: Lower resistance per metre. On very long runs, increasing conductor size is often cheaper than raising the supply voltage or moving equipment.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: An intermittent instrument fault that appears only in wet weather most often indicates:

options.B: Moisture ingress at a gland, junction box or terminal, creating a leakage path

questions.rationale: Weather-correlated faults are almost always ingress. Check gland integrity and enclosure sealing before touching the instrument.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A transmitter is 4-20 mA and HART enabled but the handheld will not connect on site, although it works on the bench. The most likely site cause is:

options.B: Insufficient loop resistance at the connection point, or excessive cable capacitance on the long run
options.C: The DCS is polling too fast

questions.rationale: HART needs at least 250 ohm and is degraded by high cable capacitance. Both are site conditions absent from a bench test.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Twisting the conductors of an instrument pair reduces noise because:

options.B: Interference couples nearly equally into both conductors and cancels in the differential receiver

questions.rationale: The twist makes the two conductors see nearly identical interference, which then cancels. It is the same principle as differential signalling on RS-485.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: An analogue input card is described as having a 250 ohm input impedance. In the loop budget this counts as:

options.B: Part of the total burden the transmitter must drive

questions.rationale: It is series resistance in the loop path and counts fully. Cards vary from 50 to 250 ohm and the actual figure matters on long runs.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: When should the loop budget be calculated on a project?

options.B: During detailed design, using the actual cable lengths, barrier types and card impedance

questions.rationale: At design, using real numbers. Discovering a budget failure at commissioning means recabling or repositioning equipment under schedule pressure.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: The valve flow coefficient Cv is defined as:

options.B: The flow of water in US gallons per minute through the valve at a pressure drop of 1 psi
options.D: The ratio of inlet to outlet pressure

questions.rationale: Cv is US gpm of water at 1 psi drop. Kv is the metric equivalent, in cubic metres per hour of water at 1 bar drop.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: The correct sizing sequence is:

options.A: Choose the valve, then check the process
options.B: Establish process conditions, calculate required Cv at each case, select a valve, then re-run the calculation to confirm
options.C: Match the valve to the line size

questions.rationale: Calculate, select, then recalculate with the chosen valve's actual data. That iterate-and-confirm step is what separates sizing from guessing.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Sizing a control valve at maximum flow only is poor practice because:

options.B: The valve may be uncontrollable at minimum flow, sitting near the seat with poor resolution

questions.rationale: You must check the minimum case too. A valve sized only for maximum ends up throttling at 5 percent travel at normal load.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A control valve should normally operate, at normal flow, at approximately:

options.B: 20 to 30 percent travel

questions.rationale: Comfortably in the mid to upper range, where gain and resolution are good and there is headroom for upsets.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Matching a control valve to the line size is:

options.B: A common error - the valve should be sized on required Cv, and is often one or two sizes smaller than the line

questions.rationale: Line size and Cv are different questions. Line-size valves are usually oversized, which is the most common valve problem in the field.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Cavitation in a control valve occurs when:

options.A: The fluid temperature exceeds boiling point
options.B: Pressure falls below the vapour pressure at the vena contracta and then recovers above it, collapsing the vapour bubbles

questions.rationale: Bubbles form at the vena contracta then implode as pressure recovers downstream. The implosions destroy trim and produce a characteristic gravel-in-a-pipe noise.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Flashing differs from cavitation in that with flashing:

options.B: The downstream pressure remains below vapour pressure, so the vapour does not collapse and a two-phase flow leaves the valve

questions.rationale: No recovery means no implosion. Flashing erodes the body and downstream pipe rather than destroying the trim, and it cannot be designed out by trim changes alone.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Choked flow in a control valve means:

options.B: Further reduction in downstream pressure produces no further increase in flow

questions.rationale: Flow limits regardless of further pressure drop. Sizing calculations that ignore choking will oversize the valve.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Select all remedies for cavitation in a control valve.

options.B: Increasing the downstream pressure by relocating the valve or adding a restriction downstream
options.C: Splitting the pressure drop across two valves in series
options.E: Harder trim material as a partial mitigation

questions.rationale: Stage the pressure drop, raise downstream pressure, or use anti-cavitation trim. Harder materials extend life but do not stop the mechanism. Increasing size makes it worse.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: The pressure recovery factor FL of a valve indicates:

options.B: How much of the pressure drop is recovered downstream, which determines its susceptibility to cavitation

questions.rationale: High recovery valves such as butterfly and ball are more prone to cavitation than low recovery globe valves at the same duty.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A globe valve has a Cv of 100 at full travel. A second valve is required with twice the capacity at the same conditions. What Cv is needed? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: Cv scales directly with capacity at the same pressure drop, so twice the flow needs twice the Cv.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: When a valve is sized, the pressure drop used should be:

options.B: The pressure drop available across the valve at that flow condition, after system losses

questions.rationale: Only the drop across the valve counts. Using the total system pressure produces a wildly undersized Cv.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A valve takes only 5 percent of the total system pressure drop at maximum flow. The consequence is:

options.B: Poor control authority - the valve has little influence over flow and its installed characteristic is severely distorted

questions.rationale: Low valve pressure drop relative to the system means the valve barely controls anything. A common rule is that the valve should take at least a quarter to a third of the total drop at maximum flow.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Noise from a control valve on gas service is primarily caused by:

options.B: Aerodynamic noise from high velocity and turbulence at high pressure drop

questions.rationale: Aerodynamic noise. Remedies include low-noise trim, staging the pressure drop, and downstream diffusers.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: When our engineer produces a valve sizing calculation for a client submission, what must accompany the Cv figure?

options.B: The process conditions used at each case, the assumptions, the selected valve's actual Cv and travel, and the noise and cavitation check

questions.rationale: A bare Cv is unreviewable. The conditions, assumptions and checks are what let a third party verify it - and what protect us if the valve underperforms.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Installed characteristic differs from inherent characteristic because:

options.B: System pressure drop redistributes as flow changes, so the valve does not see constant differential

questions.rationale: As flow rises, more of the system drop is taken by piping and less by the valve. That is what distorts the characteristic the loop actually experiences.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Valve gain is defined as:

options.A: Flow divided by travel at a point on the installed characteristic
options.B: Cv divided by line size

questions.rationale: The slope of the installed characteristic at the operating point. A loop is easiest to tune when this gain is roughly constant across the range.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Stiction in a control valve is:

options.B: The combination of static friction and sudden release, so the stem sticks then jumps past its target

questions.rationale: Stick then slip. It produces the sawtooth controller output and square-wave process variable that is the diagnostic signature of a sticking valve.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Deadband in a valve assembly is:

options.A: The range where the valve leaks
options.B: The signal change required before the stem moves at all after a reversal in direction

questions.rationale: Signal change producing no movement, particularly on direction reversal. It appears in the loop as an unresponsive region around the operating point.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A smart positioner improves loop performance mainly by:

options.B: Closing a fast local position loop that overcomes friction and hysteresis before the process loop sees them

questions.rationale: It corrects the valve's own imperfections locally and quickly, so the process controller sees a much more linear and responsive final element.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Excessive packing tightness on a control valve typically causes:

options.A: Better shutoff and no side effects
options.B: Increased friction, worse stiction and degraded control

questions.rationale: Tightening packing to stop a leak is a routine maintenance action that quietly ruins control performance. It is a frequent hidden cause of loop cycling.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Select all symptoms consistent with valve stiction rather than incorrect tuning.

options.A: Sawtooth controller output with square-wave process variable
options.B: A limit cycle that persists at any tuning setting
options.C: The cycle disappears when the controller is placed in manual
options.D: Oscillation that changes period when gain is changed
options.E: A step in output of less than one percent producing no movement

questions.rationale: Stiction cycles survive retuning and stop in manual. An oscillation whose period tracks the controller gain is a tuning problem instead.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Anti-cavitation trim works by:

options.B: Taking the pressure drop in multiple stages or through many small passages, keeping local pressure above vapour pressure

questions.rationale: Staging the pressure drop prevents the local pressure ever falling far enough for vapour to form. It prevents the mechanism rather than resisting its damage.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A desuperheater is used to:

options.B: Reduce steam temperature by injecting and evaporating water into the flow

questions.rationale: Temperature reduction by water injection. Turbine bypass and steam conditioning stations combine this with pressure reduction.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A valve in a safety instrumented function differs from a normal control valve in that it:

options.B: Must be selected and tested for its ability to move to the safe position on demand, with documented failure rate data

questions.rationale: The requirement is reliable movement to safe state on demand, evidenced by data. Its normal-service throttling performance is secondary or irrelevant.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Why is a control valve generally unsuitable as the isolation element in a shutdown function?

options.B: Its seat leakage class and its shared role with the control system compromise both tight shutoff and independence

questions.rationale: Leakage class and independence. Using the control valve as the trip element is a classic finding in a safety design review.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A valve is specified as air-to-open with a spring return. On loss of instrument air the valve will:

options.B: Close

questions.rationale: Spring drives it closed. Air-to-open equals fail closed, and the spring is what makes it deterministic.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A double-acting piston actuator without a spring or accumulator will, on loss of air:

options.B: Open
options.C: Hold its last position, which may not be safe

questions.rationale: Fail-last is not fail-safe. Where a defined safe position is required, a volume tank, an accumulator or a spring-return actuator must be specified.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Valve travel time on a shutdown valve matters because:

options.B: The safety function's response time must fit within the process safety time, and valve stroke usually dominates it
options.D: It determines the actuator size only

questions.rationale: Stroke time is usually the largest part of the response. A valve that closes in 14 seconds against an 8 second requirement fails the function regardless of its PFD.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Actuator sizing must account for:

options.B: The differential pressure the valve must close against, packing friction, and the required safety factor

questions.rationale: Shutoff differential plus friction plus margin. An actuator sized only for travel will stall against process pressure at the worst possible moment.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Under the IEC zone system, Zone 0 is an area where an explosive gas atmosphere is:

options.B: Present continuously or for long periods
options.D: Present for short periods during startup

questions.rationale: Zone 0 is continuous or long-term presence, typically inside a tank vapour space. Zone 1 is likely in normal operation; Zone 2 is unlikely and short-lived if it occurs.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Under the IEC system, Zone 2 describes an area where an explosive gas atmosphere is:

options.B: Likely during normal operation
options.C: Not likely in normal operation and, if it occurs, will persist only for a short period

questions.rationale: Zone 2 is the abnormal-only case. Most open process areas around well-maintained equipment fall here.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Zones 20, 21 and 22 apply to:

options.B: Combustible dust atmospheres

questions.rationale: The 20 series covers dust, on the same continuous, likely, unlikely logic. Relevant to our sugar, ferro alloy and grain-handling clients.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: The North American Division system relates to the IEC zone system approximately as:

options.B: Division 1 covers Zones 0 and 1; Division 2 corresponds to Zone 2

questions.rationale: Division 1 lumps together what IEC splits into Zones 0 and 1. This is why equipment certified for one system needs careful review for the other.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Under IEC, gas group IIC includes:

options.B: Propane

questions.rationale: IIC is the most easily ignited group - hydrogen and acetylene. IIA is propane and similar; IIB is ethylene.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A critical difference between IEC gas groups and NEC gas groups is that:

options.A: They use the same letters in the same order
options.B: The letter order is reversed in severity - IEC IIC is the most hazardous while NEC Group D is the least

questions.rationale: IEC runs IIA to IIC increasing in severity; NEC runs A to D decreasing. Mixing them up on an export job is dangerous, not merely embarrassing.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A temperature class of T4 means the equipment's maximum surface temperature does not exceed:

options.B: 100 degC

questions.rationale: T4 is 135 degC. T6 is the most restrictive at 85 degC and T1 the least at 450 degC.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: The temperature class required for an area is determined by:

options.B: The auto-ignition temperature of the gas present, which the equipment surface must stay below

questions.rationale: Surface temperature must stay below the gas's auto-ignition temperature. Zone tells you how often gas is present; T class tells you how hot the equipment may get.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Protection type Ex d is:

options.B: Flameproof - the enclosure contains an internal explosion and prevents its transmission

questions.rationale: Ex d contains rather than prevents. The flame path gaps are critical, which is why opening an Ex d enclosure at site is tightly controlled.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Protection type Ex i works by:

options.B: Limiting the energy available in the circuit below that needed to ignite the atmosphere
options.C: Excluding the atmosphere with clean air

questions.rationale: Energy limitation. It is the only protection type that permits live working in a hazardous area, which is its major operational advantage.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Protection type Ex p is:

options.B: Pressurisation - maintaining a clean air or inert gas overpressure to exclude the hazardous atmosphere

questions.rationale: Pressurisation, used for analyser houses and large panels. It requires purge and pressure monitoring interlocks to be a valid protection.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Select all information that must appear on a hazardous area equipment certificate or nameplate.

options.A: Protection type such as Ex d or Ex ia
options.B: Gas group
options.D: Equipment protection level or zone suitability

questions.rationale: Protection type, gas group, T class and EPL or zone. Commercial references are not part of the certification marking.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Ex ia is suitable for use in:

options.B: Zone 0, 1 and 2

questions.rationale: Ex ia tolerates two independent faults and is suitable for Zone 0. Ex ib tolerates one fault and suits Zone 1; Ex ic suits Zone 2.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Ex ic is never appropriate for a process safety function because:

options.B: It provides no fault tolerance, so a single fault can defeat the protection
options.D: It is not recognised by IEC

questions.rationale: Ex ic assumes normal operation only. A protection layer must remain safe under fault conditions, which is exactly what ic does not guarantee.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Who is responsible for classifying the hazardous areas on a plant?

options.B: The plant owner or their appointed process safety specialist, using the area classification study

questions.rationale: Classification is an owner responsibility, documented in the area classification drawings. We select equipment to suit it; we do not decide it.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A Zener barrier limits energy into the hazardous area by:

options.B: Clamping voltage with Zener diodes and limiting current with a resistor, referenced to a high-integrity earth

questions.rationale: Zener clamp plus current-limiting resistor. Its correct operation depends entirely on a reliable connection to a high-integrity earth.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A galvanic isolator differs from a Zener barrier in that it:

options.B: Provides transformer or optical isolation and does not need a high-integrity earth connection

questions.rationale: No dedicated IS earth required. That is why galvanic isolators are usually preferred despite the higher unit cost - the earth system is the expensive part.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: The IS earth for a Zener barrier system must be:

options.A: Bonded to the general plant earth at many points
options.B: A dedicated, high-integrity, low-resistance connection to a single earth reference
options.D: Connected to the cable shield only

questions.rationale: Dedicated and high integrity, with resistance typically specified below 1 ohm. A failed IS earth removes the protection silently.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: In an entity parameter comparison, the requirement for voltage is:

options.A: Uo of the barrier must be greater than Ui of the field device
options.B: Uo of the barrier must be less than or equal to Ui of the field device

questions.rationale: The barrier's maximum output must not exceed what the field device is certified to withstand. The same logic applies to current and power.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Select all entity parameter comparisons required for an intrinsically safe loop.

options.A: Uo less than or equal to Ui
options.B: Io less than or equal to Ii
options.C: Po less than or equal to Pi
options.D: Co greater than or equal to Ci plus cable capacitance
options.E: Lo greater than or equal to Li plus cable inductance

questions.rationale: All five. The cable's own capacitance and inductance must be added to the device values, which is why cable length is limited on IS circuits.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Why does cable length matter in an intrinsically safe loop verification?

options.A: It affects the 4-20 mA reading only
options.B: The cable's capacitance and inductance add to the field device's values and must remain within the barrier's permitted Co and Lo

questions.rationale: Cable stores energy too. Exceeding Co or Lo invalidates the IS certification even though the loop still works electrically.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: An IS loop verification document should record:

options.B: The barrier and field device entity parameters, the cable type and length with its capacitance and inductance, and the comparison result

questions.rationale: All the parameters and the comparison. This is a document a third-party inspector will ask for, and it must exist before energisation.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Adding a Zener barrier to a 4-20 mA loop typically consumes how much of the loop budget?

options.B: A significant series resistance and voltage drop that must be included in the calculation
options.D: Only in hazardous areas above Zone 1

questions.rationale: Barriers add hundreds of ohms of effective series resistance in some cases. Retrofitting one without redoing the budget is a common cause of a loop failing at 20 mA.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A HART handheld fails to communicate on an intrinsically safe loop that reads correctly. A likely cause is:

options.B: The barrier does not pass the HART frequencies, or the loop resistance at the connection point is below 250 ohm
options.C: The transmitter is not HART enabled

questions.rationale: Not all barriers are HART transparent. This must be checked at selection, not discovered during commissioning.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Live working on an intrinsically safe circuit in a hazardous area is:

options.B: Permitted, because the circuit's energy is limited below ignition capability - which is the main operational advantage of IS
options.D: Permitted only with a gas test

questions.rationale: This is the practical reason IS is chosen. With Ex d you must isolate and often obtain a gas-free certificate before opening the enclosure.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: IS field wiring must be identified by:

options.B: Light blue sheath or clear marking, and segregation from non-IS wiring

questions.rationale: Light blue by convention, with physical segregation. Mixing IS and non-IS wiring in one bundle defeats the protection by allowing energy transfer.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: Minimum separation between IS and non-IS terminals in a marshalling panel is required because:

options.B: A fault could transfer energy from a non-IS circuit into the IS circuit, defeating the energy limitation

questions.rationale: Energy transfer under fault conditions. Standards specify a minimum separation, typically 50 mm, or a physical partition.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: A client's existing loop uses a Zener barrier and the IS earth measures 8 ohm. Your position should be:

options.B: Non-compliant against the usual requirement of well under 1 ohm - report it as a finding, since the IS protection is compromised
options.D: Acceptable if the loop reads correctly

questions.rationale: The loop reading correctly proves nothing about the protection. A degraded IS earth is a live safety finding and must be reported in writing.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: For a new project in a Zone 1 area with a long cable run and many loops, which protection approach usually gives the lowest total installed cost?

options.A: Ex d throughout with heavy conduit
options.B: Intrinsic safety using galvanic isolators, avoiding both the IS earth system and the Ex d installation cost
options.C: Zener barriers with a dedicated earth grid

questions.rationale: Galvanic isolators avoid the dedicated earth system and the conduit and gland cost of Ex d. The unit price is higher and the installed cost usually lower.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: When our offer includes hazardous area equipment, the deviation most worth stating explicitly is:

options.B: That equipment selection is based on the area classification drawings supplied by the client, and changes to classification will change the scope and price

questions.rationale: Our selection depends entirely on their classification. Stating that dependency protects us when the classification is revised after award, which happens regularly.
questions.category: Field Instrumentation, Final Control Elements & Loop Engineering

questions.question: SCADA stands for:

options.B: Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition

questions.rationale: Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition. The word supervisory is the key - it oversees, it does not usually close fast control loops itself.

questions.question: The word supervisory in SCADA implies that:

options.B: It oversees and coordinates control that is largely executed by local devices such as PLCs and RTUs
options.E: It is a management reporting tool

questions.rationale: Local devices do the closed-loop work; SCADA supervises, sets targets and gathers data. That division is what lets a SCADA survive a communications outage.

questions.question: Before software-based SCADA, plants were supervised using:

options.B: Panel boards of hardwired indicators, recorders and selector switches

questions.rationale: Relay panels and instrument boards. Understanding that lineage explains why many SCADA conventions look the way they do.

questions.question: An RTU in a SCADA system is:

options.A: A remote terminal unit that acquires data and executes control at a remote site
options.B: A relay test unit

questions.rationale: Remote Terminal Unit. It sits at a geographically distant site, gathers data locally and reports back to the supervisory layer.

questions.question: Which of these is a typical SCADA application?

options.B: A water distribution network spread across a city

questions.rationale: Geographically dispersed assets are the classic SCADA case - water networks, pipelines, power distribution.

questions.question: A tag in a SCADA system is:

options.A: A physical label on a cable
options.B: A named data point representing a value or status in the system

questions.rationale: A named data point. The tag database is the backbone of the system and drives licensing, historian sizing and graphics.

questions.question: A trend display in a SCADA system shows:

options.B: How one or more values have changed over time

questions.rationale: Values over time. Trends are the single most useful diagnostic tool available to an operator or a commissioning engineer.

questions.question: Polling in a SCADA system means:

options.B: The supervisory system requesting data from each remote device in turn

questions.rationale: Sequential requests to each device. Polling is simple but means a value is only as fresh as the last scan of that device.

questions.question: Store and forward at an RTU means the RTU:

options.A: Buffers data locally during a communications outage and sends it when the link is restored
options.B: Forwards all data immediately

questions.rationale: Local buffering preserves the historical record through a link failure. This is why SCADA suits remote sites with unreliable communications.

questions.question: A SCADA system's data acquisition function primarily serves to:

options.B: Gather process and equipment data for display, alarming, recording and reporting

questions.rationale: Acquire, display, alarm, record, report. The control itself normally sits closer to the process.

questions.question: A mimic or graphic display in a SCADA system is:

options.B: A schematic representation of the process with live values and status overlaid

questions.rationale: A schematic with live data. It is a working tool, not a picture, and that distinction drives everything in high performance HMI design.

questions.question: Which function is normally NOT performed by the SCADA layer itself?

options.B: Recording historical data

questions.rationale: Safety interlocks belong in a dedicated safety system, not in the supervisory layer. Speed and independence both argue against it.

questions.question: DCS stands for:

options.B: Distributed Control System

questions.rationale: Distributed Control System. Distributed refers to the controllers being spread through the plant rather than centralised.

questions.question: The primary orientation of a DCS is:

options.A: Data gathering across a wide area
options.B: Process control within a single facility, tightly integrated with the process

questions.rationale: A DCS is process-oriented and tightly coupled to one facility. SCADA is data-acquisition oriented across dispersed sites.

questions.question: Which is more typical of a DCS installation?

options.B: A continuous chemical plant on one site
options.D: A network of unmanned pumping stations

questions.rationale: A single continuous process facility. The others are geographically dispersed, which is SCADA territory.

questions.question: In a DCS, control loops are typically executed:

options.B: In distributed controllers close to the process, at a deterministic scan rate

questions.rationale: In the controllers, deterministically. This is why a DCS can be relied on for regulatory control in a way a polled SCADA cannot.

questions.question: A DCS is generally described as tightly coupled. This means:

options.B: The controllers, IO, communications and operator interface are designed as one integrated system
options.C: The loops are all in cascade

questions.rationale: Designed and supplied as one integrated system, which gives consistent behaviour, consistent engineering tools and predictable performance.

questions.question: SCADA systems are often described as loosely coupled because:

options.B: They integrate devices from many vendors over standard protocols and tolerate communication interruptions

questions.rationale: Multi-vendor integration and tolerance of link loss are strengths for dispersed assets, not weaknesses.

questions.question: Which system would you expect to handle a communications outage to a remote site more gracefully?

options.B: SCADA, because remote units are designed to operate autonomously and buffer data

questions.rationale: SCADA assumes the link may fail. A DCS assumes it will not, which is reasonable within one plant and unreasonable across 400 km.

questions.question: For a captive power plant on the same site as the process it serves, the natural choice is:

options.B: A DCS, because it is a continuous process in a single facility requiring tight, deterministic control

questions.rationale: Single site, continuous process, tight control - the classic DCS case. That it involves power generation does not change the architecture question.

questions.question: The distinction between DCS and SCADA has blurred in recent years mainly because:

options.B: Both now use similar hardware, networks and software, so the difference is increasingly about architecture and application rather than technology

questions.rationale: The technology converged; the architectural intent did not. Being able to articulate the remaining difference matters commercially for us.

questions.question: When a client asks why they should buy a DCS rather than a PLC and SCADA package, the strongest technical answer concerns:

options.B: Integrated engineering, consistent control execution, built-in redundancy and a single coherent database across control, alarms and history

questions.rationale: Integration and coherence. A collection of separately engineered parts can be made to work, but the engineering effort and the lifetime maintenance burden are higher.

questions.question: Which statement about the DCS and SCADA distinction is most accurate?

options.B: DCS cannot acquire data
options.C: The distinction is one of architecture, scope and coupling rather than of capability
options.D: They are the same product with different names

questions.rationale: Architecture, scope and coupling. Both can display, alarm, record and control; they are optimised for different problems.

questions.question: In a typical SCADA architecture, the layer closest to the process is:

options.B: The field devices - sensors, transmitters and final elements

questions.rationale: Field devices are the bottom of the stack. Everything above them depends on the quality of what they measure.

questions.question: Between the field devices and the supervisory layer sits:

options.B: The control layer of PLCs or RTUs

questions.rationale: PLCs or RTUs acquire the field signals and execute local logic. The supervisory layer talks to them, not to the transmitters directly.

questions.question: The engineering station in a SCADA system is used to:

options.A: Operate the plant day to day
options.B: Configure the database, graphics, alarms and logic

questions.rationale: Configuration, not operation. Separating engineering and operator functions is both good practice and a security requirement.

questions.question: Server redundancy in a SCADA system provides:

options.B: Continuity of supervision if one server fails, with the standby taking over

questions.rationale: Continuity. The value lies in the operator never losing visibility, which matters most precisely when something is going wrong.

questions.question: A historian in a SCADA architecture is responsible for:

options.B: Recording time-stamped process data for later retrieval and analysis

questions.rationale: Time-series recording and retrieval. It is not part of the control or safety path.

questions.question: A thin client or view-only node is typically used:

options.A: In the control room for primary operation
options.B: Where staff need to see plant status but must not be able to change anything

questions.rationale: Read-only visibility for managers, maintenance or laboratory staff. It reduces both licence cost and the risk of an accidental operator action.

questions.question: Time synchronisation across a SCADA system matters because:

options.B: Sequence of events and alarm records are only meaningful if all devices share a common time reference

questions.rationale: Without common time you cannot reconstruct what happened first. Post-incident analysis depends entirely on it.

questions.question: User roles and access levels in a SCADA system exist to:

options.B: Ensure each person can perform only the actions appropriate to their role, and that actions are attributable

questions.rationale: Appropriate permissions plus attribution. An unattributable setpoint change is a problem both for safety and for accountability.

questions.question: Which architectural feature most directly limits how much history a SCADA system can retain?

options.B: Historian storage capacity together with the scan rate and compression settings

questions.rationale: Storage, scan rate and compression together determine retention. Logging every tag every second for ten years is a decision with a large and permanent cost.

questions.question: Where does the operator interface sit in the architecture?

options.B: At the supervisory layer, presenting data acquired from the control layer
options.E: Between the sensors and the PLC

questions.rationale: The supervisory layer. The HMI is a window onto data acquired below it, which is why an HMI failure should not stop the plant controlling.

questions.question: If the link between the supervisory layer and a PLC fails, a well-designed system will:

options.B: Continue local control at the PLC while the operator loses visibility, and alarm the loss of communication clearly
options.C: Freeze the PLC outputs at zero

questions.rationale: Local control continues and the loss is annunciated. Losing the view is serious; losing control because you lost the view would be a design fault.

questions.question: The relationship between an HMI and a SCADA system is that:

options.B: The HMI is the operator interface component of a SCADA system, not a separate competing system
options.C: SCADA is a type of HMI

questions.rationale: The HMI is a component. Treating them as alternatives is a terminology error our engineers should never make in front of a client.

questions.question: A local panel-mounted HMI on a packaged skid typically provides:

options.B: Local operation and monitoring of that skid only
options.C: Historical archiving for the whole plant

questions.rationale: Local scope. It is an operator interface for one machine or skid, with no supervisory role beyond it.

questions.question: Which capability distinguishes a SCADA system from a standalone HMI?

options.B: Supervision of multiple distributed units with centralised alarming, historical archiving and reporting

questions.rationale: Scope and centralisation. Both display values; only one supervises a whole system.

questions.question: Both HMI and SCADA systems must handle alarms because:

options.B: The operator needs to be told about abnormal conditions requiring a response, whatever the scope of the system
options.E: Standards require it only for SCADA

questions.rationale: Any system an operator relies on must tell them when something needs attention. That obligation does not scale away on a small system.

questions.question: A faceplate in an HMI is:

options.A: The physical bezel of the screen
options.B: A standard pop-up giving detailed information and control for one device or loop

questions.rationale: A consistent pop-up per device type. Consistency across faceplates is what lets an operator use an unfamiliar loop correctly under pressure.

questions.question: Why should faceplates be consistent across an entire HMI?

options.B: So an operator's learned behaviour transfers to every device, which matters most during an upset

questions.rationale: Learned behaviour must transfer. Under stress the operator falls back on habit, and inconsistent faceplates turn habit into error.

questions.question: An operator action on an HMI should be:

options.B: Attributable to a named user and, for significant actions, logged and where appropriate confirmed

questions.rationale: Attributable and logged. Anonymous shared logins defeat both accountability and any subsequent incident investigation.

questions.question: Which is a legitimate reason to use a local HMI as well as a central SCADA on the same equipment?

options.B: To allow local operation and maintenance at the equipment, particularly during commissioning and fault finding
options.D: To avoid the need for user roles

questions.rationale: Local operation during commissioning and maintenance is a genuine need. It must not become an uncontrolled second point of command during normal operation.

questions.question: When a client says they want an HMI but describes centralised alarming, historian and multi-unit supervision, they actually need:

options.B: A SCADA or DCS system - and the terminology should be clarified before quoting

questions.rationale: Clarify the terminology before quoting. Quoting an HMI against a SCADA requirement is the kind of misunderstanding that surfaces at FAT.

questions.question: A screen showing a live schematic of a distillation column with valve positions and temperatures is:

options.B: A process graphic or mimic

questions.rationale: A process graphic. Faceplates, trends, alarm summaries and reports are separate display types with separate purposes.

questions.question: The fundamental purpose of the operator interface is to:

options.B: Give the operator the information needed to understand the plant's state and act correctly

questions.rationale: Understanding and correct action. Every design decision in the next levels follows from taking that purpose seriously.

questions.question: Under ISA-18.2, an alarm is defined as an indication of a condition that:

options.B: Requires a timely operator response
options.C: Has been configured in the system

questions.rationale: Requiring a timely operator response is the defining test. A condition needing no response is information, not an alarm.

questions.question: The single most useful test of whether something should be an alarm is:

options.B: Is there a defined operator action, and is there time to take it?

questions.rationale: Defined action plus available time. If the operator can do nothing about it, an alarm only adds noise.

questions.question: An alarm flood is commonly defined as:

options.B: More than 10 alarms in 10 minutes for one operator

questions.rationale: More than 10 in 10 minutes per operator. Beyond that rate the operator cannot process them, so the system has effectively stopped communicating.

questions.question: Why do alarm floods occur most often at exactly the wrong moment?

options.B: A single upset propagates through the plant, tripping many correlated alarms just when the operator most needs clarity

questions.rationale: One root cause produces many correlated alarms. The flood peaks during the upset, which is precisely when the operator needs to identify the cause.

questions.question: The most common root cause of an overloaded alarm system is:

options.B: Alarms configured on every available point during engineering, without asking what the operator would do about each one

questions.rationale: Configuring alarms because the point exists rather than because a response exists. It costs nothing at engineering stage and everything in operation.

questions.question: A chattering alarm is one that:

options.B: Repeatedly transitions between active and clear in a short period

questions.rationale: Rapid repeated transitions, usually from a noisy measurement sitting on its setpoint. Deadband or an on-delay normally fixes it.

questions.question: A stale alarm is one that:

options.B: Has remained in the active state for an extended period, commonly more than 24 hours

questions.rationale: Active for over 24 hours. It teaches the operator to ignore that part of the display, which then hides a genuine new alarm.

questions.question: Select all valid techniques for eliminating a chattering alarm.

options.A: Adding deadband so the alarm must clear by a margin before it can reactivate
options.B: Adding an on-delay so a brief excursion does not raise the alarm
options.D: Investigating and fixing the noisy measurement or the underlying process cause

questions.rationale: Deadband, delay, or fix the underlying cause. Raising priority makes it worse, and indefinite shelving hides a real condition.

questions.question: Alarm priority should be determined by:

options.A: The order the alarms were configured
options.B: The severity of the consequence and the time available for the operator to respond
options.D: The seniority of the requesting engineer

questions.rationale: Consequence severity and available response time together. Priority is a statement about urgency, not about how important the equipment feels.

questions.question: A typical target distribution of alarm priorities is approximately:

options.A: Equal thirds across low, medium and high
options.B: Around 80 percent low, 15 percent medium and 5 percent high

questions.rationale: Roughly 80/15/5. When most alarms are high priority, priority has stopped conveying any information at all.

questions.question: Historically, deficient alarm management has been identified as a contributing factor in:

options.B: Major process incidents including Three Mile Island, Milford Haven and Texas City
