options.B: Gives a common vocabulary for where Miralys sits relative to the control layer and the business layer when explaining the architecture to a client

questions.rationale: A shared vocabulary for positioning. Being able to place a product precisely in a model the client already uses is a commercial advantage.

questions.question: A Factory Acceptance Test is performed:

options.B: At the manufacturer's works before shipment, against the approved design documents

questions.rationale: At the works, before shipment, against approved documents. Finding a fault there costs a fraction of finding it at site.

questions.question: A Site Acceptance Test differs from a FAT in that the SAT:

options.B: Tests the installed system with real field connections in its final environment

questions.rationale: Real installation, real field wiring, real environment. It verifies what the FAT could only simulate.

questions.question: A System Integration Test is concerned with:

options.B: The correct interaction of multiple subsystems once they are connected together

questions.rationale: Interaction between subsystems. Each package can pass its own FAT and the assembly still fail at the interfaces.

questions.question: The FAT should be conducted against:

options.B: The approved FDS, cause and effect matrix, IO list and control philosophy

questions.rationale: The approved documents. Without an agreed basis a FAT becomes a negotiation about what was intended.

questions.question: Select all items that should be confirmed during a control system FAT.

options.A: Every I/O point responds correctly to a simulated signal
options.B: Control logic and interlocks match the cause and effect matrix
options.C: Graphics, alarms and reports match the FDS

questions.rationale: IO, logic, HMI and redundancy. Field cable testing can only be done at site during pre-commissioning.

questions.question: Poor panel workmanship discovered at FAT should be:

options.A: Accepted with a note, since function is unaffected
options.B: Treated as a finding, because it usually indicates weaker fabrication quality control generally
options.C: Ignored if the client does not notice

questions.rationale: Workmanship is a proxy for process quality. Waving it through at FAT means you are also waving through whatever else that process produced.

questions.question: The most common fault found at site that should have been found at FAT is:

options.B: Loose terminations

questions.rationale: Loose terminations. A systematic torque and tug check before shipment removes a whole class of site problems.

questions.question: A punch list item raised at FAT should record:

options.B: The item, the responsible party, the agreed action and the target date for closure

questions.rationale: Item, owner, action and date. A list without owners and dates is a list of complaints, not a plan.

questions.question: A client waives attendance at the FAT. This means:

options.A: The FAT need not be performed
options.B: The FAT must still be performed and documented, since it is a required stage in the quality plan
options.D: The documents need not be approved

questions.rationale: Attendance and performance are different things. The test is a quality plan requirement regardless of who watches it.

questions.question: Referencing specific standard clauses, such as IEC 62443 requirements, in our FAT procedure is worthwhile because:

options.B: It demonstrates to an EPC that our testing is systematic and traceable to recognised requirements rather than ad hoc

questions.rationale: It converts our test procedure from an internal habit into a demonstrable, auditable process. That is cheap credibility with a technically demanding client.

questions.question: The relationship between the FAT and the ITP is that the FAT is:

options.B: One gate event within the Inspection and Test Plan, which is itself part of the quality plan
options.C: The document that governs the ITP
options.E: Issued after the ITP is closed

questions.rationale: The FAT is one event inside the ITP. A buyer may waive attendance at the FAT but cannot waive the ITP requirement itself.

questions.question: In an ITP, a Hold point means:

options.A: Work may proceed if the inspector does not attend
options.B: Work must stop until the specified party has inspected and released it
options.D: The item is on hold commercially

questions.rationale: Work stops until released. A Witness point allows work to proceed if the inspector does not attend, provided the record is made; a Review point is documentary only.

questions.question: A process historian is best described as:

options.A: A relational database with timestamps added
options.B: A database optimised for storing and retrieving large volumes of time-stamped process values
options.D: A backup of the control system configuration

questions.rationale: It is optimised for time-series data specifically. General-purpose databases can store the same values but retrieve them far more slowly over long time ranges.

questions.question: The three items normally stored with every historian sample are:

options.B: Timestamp, value and quality

questions.rationale: Timestamp, value and quality. The quality code is what makes the data auditable rather than merely numerical.

questions.question: A quality code of Bad on a historian value means:

options.A: The value is outside its alarm limits
options.B: The value could not be reliably obtained, for example because the source device failed or communication was lost

questions.rationale: It marks the reading as unreliable. Without it, a failed sensor's last value silently becomes a data point in every report.

questions.question: Why does the quality code matter when a reporting system averages a value over a shift?

options.B: Averaging bad or stale readings into a KPI produces a confident but wrong number

questions.rationale: Bad data averaged into a KPI is worse than no report at all, because it is believed. Filtering on quality is a basic requirement of any reporting layer.

questions.question: A historian's tag-based schema means data is organised primarily by:

options.B: The point being measured, with values indexed by time

questions.rationale: Tag then time. That structure is what makes retrieving one tag over a year fast, which is the query historians exist to serve.

questions.question: The main reason a DCS cannot serve as its own long-term historian is that:

options.B: Controllers hold only minutes of data and their storage and processing are dedicated to control

questions.rationale: Controllers keep a short buffer only. Their job is control, and loading them with archival storage would compromise it.

questions.question: Retention policy in a historian defines:

options.B: How long data is kept, and at what resolution, before it is aggregated or deleted

questions.rationale: How long and at what resolution. Keeping everything at full resolution forever is a decision with a large and permanent cost.

questions.question: A typical use of historian data by a process engineer is:

options.B: Investigating why a batch went off specification by comparing it against previous good batches

questions.rationale: Comparison against history is what turns raw data into an answer. It is the single most common analytical use of a historian.

questions.question: Historian data is used for troubleshooting a trip because:

options.A: It replaces the sequence of events record
options.B: It shows how each variable was behaving before, during and after the event, at a resolution the operator display cannot provide after the fact

questions.rationale: It is the record of what actually happened. Without it, post-trip analysis relies on recollection.

questions.question: A historian sits at which point relative to the control system?

options.B: Above the control layer, reading data from it, with no role in the control or safety path
options.E: Between the sensor and the IO card

questions.rationale: Above the control layer, reading only. A historian failure must never be able to affect control.

questions.question: When quoting a historian, the parameter that most directly drives cost is usually:

options.B: The number of tags, and in some licensing models the sampling rate and retention

questions.rationale: Tag count is the primary licensing and sizing driver. Establishing it accurately before quoting avoids a difficult conversation later.

questions.question: Exception reporting in a historian means a value is:

options.B: Stored only when it changes by more than a defined deadband
options.C: Stored only when an alarm occurs

questions.rationale: A value only enters the system when it has moved beyond the deadband. This is compression at the collection stage.
questions.moduleTopic: Compression, and what it costs you

questions.question: Swinging door compression works by:

options.B: Storing only the endpoints of segments that can be reconstructed by a straight line within a defined tolerance
options.E: Compressing the file with a general-purpose algorithm

questions.rationale: It fits a line and stores only the points needed to reconstruct it within tolerance. It is compression at the archival stage.
questions.moduleTopic: Compression, and what it costs you

questions.question: Together, exception reporting and swinging door compression typically reduce stored volume by:

options.B: Around 20 percent
options.C: An order of magnitude or more

questions.rationale: An order of magnitude or more is normal on process data, because most process values are steady most of the time.
questions.moduleTopic: Compression, and what it costs you

questions.question: The cost of setting compression tolerances too wide is that:

options.B: Short events such as spikes and brief excursions are erased and cannot be recovered

questions.rationale: Compression is lossy and irreversible. The short events erased are exactly the ones needed to diagnose an upset.
questions.moduleTopic: Compression, and what it costs you

questions.question: Compression settings should be chosen based on:

options.A: A single value applied to all tags
options.B: The noise characteristics and the analytical purpose of each individual tag

questions.rationale: Per tag, based on noise and intended use. A blanket setting either wastes storage on quiet tags or destroys detail on important ones.
questions.moduleTopic: Compression, and what it costs you

questions.question: Which tag would justify tighter compression than a slowly varying tank level?

options.B: A pressure signal on a compressor where short transients are diagnostically important

questions.rationale: Fast transients need fine resolution. A tank level moving over hours does not.
questions.moduleTopic: Compression, and what it costs you

questions.question: A plant logs 10000 tags at one sample per second. How many raw values are generated per hour? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: 10000 multiplied by 3600 seconds equals 36,000,000 raw values per hour. This is why compression exists.
questions.moduleTopic: Compression, and what it costs you

questions.question: If compression reduces the stored count to 5 percent of the raw values, how many values are stored per hour from those 10000 tags? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: 5 percent of 36,000,000 is 1,800,000. A twentyfold reduction is typical on process data.
questions.moduleTopic: Compression, and what it costs you

questions.question: A trend retrieved from a compressed historian appears as straight lines between widely spaced points. This indicates:

options.B: Compression has removed intermediate detail, which is expected behaviour, not an error

questions.rationale: That is compression working as designed. Whether the remaining detail is sufficient is a separate and important question.
questions.moduleTopic: Compression, and what it costs you

questions.question: Compression is described as lossy. This means:

options.B: The removed intermediate values cannot be recovered afterwards, only interpolated

questions.rationale: Irreversible. Once compressed away, a value is gone - which is why the settings deserve engineering attention rather than defaults.
questions.moduleTopic: Compression, and what it costs you

questions.question: A safety or regulatory investigation later requires uncompressed data that was compressed away. The correct preventive measure would have been to:

options.B: Identify regulatory and safety-critical tags at design and configure them with minimal or no compression

questions.rationale: Identify the critical tags up front. It is a design decision, and it cannot be corrected retrospectively.
questions.moduleTopic: Compression, and what it costs you

questions.question: OT stands for:

options.B: Optimised Throughput

questions.rationale: Operational Technology - the systems that monitor and control physical processes, as distinct from IT.
questions.moduleTopic: IT versus OT, and the Purdue levels

questions.question: The classic IT security priority order is confidentiality, integrity, availability. In OT the order is usually:

options.B: Effectively reversed, with safety and availability taking priority

questions.rationale: Safety and availability come first in OT. A control system that is perfectly confidential but unavailable has failed at its actual job.
questions.moduleTopic: IT versus OT, and the Purdue levels

questions.question: In the Purdue model, Level 0 is:

options.B: The physical process, including sensors and actuators

questions.rationale: Level 0 is the process and its field devices. The levels count upward from there toward the business.
questions.moduleTopic: IT versus OT, and the Purdue levels

questions.question: Level 2 in the Purdue model represents:

options.B: Area supervisory control - HMI, SCADA and engineering workstations

questions.rationale: Level 2 is supervisory control. Level 1 is the controllers and Level 3 is site operations and manufacturing operations management.
questions.moduleTopic: IT versus OT, and the Purdue levels

questions.question: In the Purdue model, which level number is conventionally assigned to the industrial DMZ? Enter the number, using a decimal point if required.
questions.rationale: Level 3.5, between site operations at Level 3 and the enterprise at Level 4. It is not in the original model but is now standard practice.
questions.moduleTopic: IT versus OT, and the Purdue levels

questions.question: The single most important architectural principle in the Purdue model is that:

options.B: There should be no direct routable path between the enterprise network and the control network
options.C: All levels use the same protocol

questions.rationale: No direct routable IT to OT path. Traffic crosses through the DMZ where it can be inspected, brokered and controlled.
questions.moduleTopic: IT versus OT, and the Purdue levels

questions.question: Patching practice differs between IT and OT because:

options.B: OT patches must be validated and applied in planned outage windows, since an unexpected restart or behaviour change can stop production or cause a trip
options.D: OT vendors do not issue patches

questions.rationale: A patch that reboots a controller is a production event. Validation and outage scheduling are why OT patching lags IT.
questions.moduleTopic: IT versus OT, and the Purdue levels

questions.question: Which incident is commonly cited as an example of an IT-side compromise causing an OT shutdown?

options.B: Colonial Pipeline

questions.rationale: Colonial Pipeline was an IT ransomware event, but operations were halted. It illustrates why the IT to OT boundary matters even when OT is not directly attacked.
questions.moduleTopic: IT versus OT, and the Purdue levels

questions.question: Triton, also known as Trisis, is notable because it:

options.B: Targeted a safety instrumented system specifically

questions.rationale: It targeted the SIS, which is the layer that exists to prevent physical harm. That is why it changed how the industry regards OT security.
questions.moduleTopic: IT versus OT, and the Purdue levels

questions.question: An engineering laptop moved between the office network and the control network represents:

options.B: A bypass of the segmentation, since it carries a routable path across the boundary in its own storage and configuration
options.C: No risk if antivirus is installed

questions.rationale: A laptop is a mobile bridge across the boundary. Dedicated OT engineering machines are a basic control, and one that is routinely ignored.
questions.moduleTopic: IT versus OT, and the Purdue levels

questions.question: When a client's IT department proposes applying their standard enterprise patching policy to our DCS, the correct response is:

options.B: Explain that OT patching requires vendor validation and planned outage windows, and propose a joint policy that addresses both security and availability
options.E: Disconnect the DCS from the network

questions.rationale: Neither compliance nor refusal. Proposing a joint policy is what converts a conflict into a technical discussion we can lead.
questions.moduleTopic: IT versus OT, and the Purdue levels

questions.question: Polled collection means the historian:

options.A: Waits for the device to send data
options.B: Requests values from the source on a fixed schedule

questions.rationale: Scheduled requests. The value is only ever as fresh as the last poll of that source.

questions.question: Unsolicited or exception-based collection means the source:

options.B: Sends a value only when it changes beyond a configured deadband

questions.rationale: The source pushes changes. It is far more efficient than polling and gives lower latency on the values that actually moved.

questions.question: The main advantage of exception-based collection over polling is:

options.B: Much lower network and processing load, with better time resolution on values that change

questions.rationale: Less traffic and better resolution where it matters. A steady tag consumes almost nothing; a moving tag is captured promptly.

questions.question: Collection deadband differs from archival compression in that the deadband:

options.B: Filters at the point of collection, so the value never enters the system at all

questions.rationale: Deadband filters on the way in; compression filters on the way to the archive. Both are lossy and both must be configured deliberately.

questions.question: Select all consequences of setting the collection deadband too wide on a control-critical tag.

options.B: Post-incident analysis of that tag becomes impossible
options.D: Loop tuning analysis from historian data becomes unreliable
options.E: The control loop itself is degraded

questions.rationale: It saves storage and destroys diagnostic value. It does not affect the control loop, which reads from the controller and not the historian.

questions.question: Time synchronisation across data sources matters to a historian because:

options.B: Values from different sources can only be compared or correlated if they share a common time reference

questions.rationale: Without common time you cannot say what happened first. Every sequence-of-events analysis depends on it.

questions.question: NTP typically achieves synchronisation accuracy of the order of:

options.B: Milliseconds

questions.rationale: Milliseconds, which is adequate for most process historian purposes. PTP is used where sub-microsecond accuracy is required.

questions.question: PTP, defined in IEEE 1588, is used instead of NTP where:

options.B: Sub-microsecond accuracy is required, such as for electrical sequence-of-events in substations

questions.rationale: Substation and power applications need microsecond ordering to determine which protection operated first. That is beyond NTP's capability.

questions.question: OPC UA historical access allows a client to:

options.B: Read stored historical values from a server over a standard interface

questions.rationale: Standardised historical read. It removes the need for a proprietary connector for every source and destination pairing.

questions.question: A store-and-forward buffer at a collection node exists to:

options.B: Retain data locally during a link failure and send it when the connection is restored

questions.rationale: Buffering preserves the record through an outage. Without it a network failure produces a permanent hole in the history.

questions.question: A gap in the historical record with good quality either side and bad quality across the gap indicates:

options.B: A collection or communication interruption that was correctly flagged rather than silently interpolated

questions.rationale: The quality flag makes the gap honest. A system that interpolates across an outage without flagging it is producing fiction.

questions.question: Two historians on the same plant report different totals for the same production figure. The first thing to check is:

options.B: Whether they collect at different rates or deadbands, and whether their time references agree

questions.rationale: Collection rate, deadband and time reference explain most such discrepancies. It is rarely a fault and usually a configuration difference.

questions.question: Calculated or derived tags in a historian should be:

options.B: Documented with their formula and source tags, so a later reader can verify what the number means

questions.rationale: An undocumented calculated tag becomes an unverifiable number in a report. Formula and sources must be recorded.

questions.question: Historian sizing should be estimated from:

options.B: Tag count, collection rate, expected compression ratio and retention period

questions.rationale: Those four parameters determine the volume. Estimating from tag count alone routinely underestimates by an order of magnitude.

questions.question: When quoting a historian for a client with 6000 tags but no stated retention requirement, we should:

options.B: Query the retention and resolution requirements, since they drive storage, licensing and cost more than tag count alone

questions.rationale: Retention and resolution must be established before quoting. Two projects with identical tag counts can differ by a factor of ten in storage.

questions.question: The primary role of a SCADA system with respect to data is to:

options.B: Visualise current state and hold a limited window of recent history

questions.rationale: SCADA visualises and keeps a short window. Long-term archival is the historian's job.
questions.moduleTopic: Historian versus SCADA versus MES versus data lake

questions.question: An MES is primarily concerned with:

options.B: Production orders, scheduling, material genealogy, quality and OEE

questions.rationale: Manufacturing operations management. It answers what was made, when, from what, and how well - not what the pressure was at 14:32.
questions.moduleTopic: Historian versus SCADA versus MES versus data lake

questions.question: A data lake differs from a historian in that a data lake:

options.B: Stores raw data of many types with schema applied on read, rather than being optimised for time-series retrieval

questions.rationale: Generic storage, schema on read. It is flexible and slow for the queries a historian is built for.
questions.moduleTopic: Historian versus SCADA versus MES versus data lake

questions.question: Which system is the authoritative raw source that typically feeds the others?

options.B: The historian, fed from the control layer

questions.rationale: The historian holds the raw time-series record. MES, reporting and analytics generally consume from it rather than from the controllers directly.
questions.moduleTopic: Historian versus SCADA versus MES versus data lake

questions.question: Select all statements that are true about the boundaries between these systems.

options.A: SCADA holds limited history, not a long-term archive
options.B: MES handles orders and genealogy rather than time-series storage
options.C: A data lake is not optimised for time-range queries on a single tag
options.E: Context enrichment links time-series values to plant structure and tag metadata

questions.rationale: All except scheduling, which belongs to MES. Being able to draw these boundaries clearly in a client meeting is a commercial advantage.
questions.moduleTopic: Historian versus SCADA versus MES versus data lake

questions.question: Context enrichment of historian data means:

options.B: Linking each time-series value to tag metadata and plant structure so it can be interpreted without external knowledge

questions.rationale: Values without context are numbers. Linking them to equipment, units and hierarchy is what makes them analysable by someone who was not there.
questions.moduleTopic: Historian versus SCADA versus MES versus data lake

questions.question: A client asks for OEE reporting. The system that naturally owns this is:

options.B: The MES layer, consuming data from the historian and the control system

questions.rationale: OEE combines availability, performance and quality, which requires order and product context that lives at the MES layer.
questions.moduleTopic: Historian versus SCADA versus MES versus data lake

questions.question: When a client says they want a historian but describes production scheduling and material genealogy, they actually need:

options.B: MES functionality, and the terminology should be clarified before quoting

questions.rationale: Clarify before quoting. Quoting a historian against an MES requirement is a scope mismatch that surfaces after award.
questions.moduleTopic: Historian versus SCADA versus MES versus data lake

questions.question: Sending raw historian data directly to a data lake without context is a common mistake because:

options.B: The values arrive without meaning, and reconstructing the context later is far harder than exporting it at source

questions.rationale: Context is cheap to attach at source and expensive to reconstruct later. This is the most common failure in industrial data projects.
questions.moduleTopic: Historian versus SCADA versus MES versus data lake

questions.question: For Miralys, the clearest architectural position to explain to a client is that it:

options.B: Sits above the control layer, consuming and contextualising process data for visualisation, reporting and supervisory purposes

questions.rationale: Being able to state precisely where a product sits, using the client's own reference model, is worth more in a meeting than a feature list.
questions.moduleTopic: Historian versus SCADA versus MES versus data lake

questions.question: A reporting layer should filter on data quality because:

options.B: Bad or stale readings averaged into a report produce a confident and wrong number

questions.rationale: Quality filtering is what stops a failed sensor becoming a plausible KPI. It is a two-line change that prevents a class of embarrassing errors.
questions.moduleTopic: Historian versus SCADA versus MES versus data lake

questions.question: Which layer should be authoritative for the production total that appears in a monthly report?

options.B: One system, explicitly designated, with the others deriving from it
options.D: The one with the highest number

questions.rationale: Explicit ownership prevents two systems producing different numbers with nobody able to say which is right.
questions.moduleTopic: Historian versus SCADA versus MES versus data lake

questions.question: A historian should never be placed in the control path because:

options.B: A failure or overload in a non-control system must not be able to affect control or safety

questions.rationale: Control must not depend on anything above it. This principle governs the whole data architecture.
questions.moduleTopic: Historian versus SCADA versus MES versus data lake

questions.question: A client wants analytics on ten years of data but has only two years archived at full resolution. The realistic answer is:

options.B: Explain what is actually available at what resolution, and design the analysis around it while improving retention going forward

questions.rationale: State what exists honestly and design around it. Data that was compressed away cannot be recovered, and pretending otherwise is worse than the gap.
questions.moduleTopic: Historian versus SCADA versus MES versus data lake

questions.question: The commercial opportunity for ArkIO in this boundary confusion is that:

options.A: Clients will pay more if confused
options.B: Clients frequently do not know which layer they need, and a clear architectural explanation positions us as the party who understands their problem

questions.rationale: Clarity is the differentiator. The party who explains the architecture usually gets to define it.
questions.moduleTopic: Historian versus SCADA versus MES versus data lake

questions.question: A Unified Namespace is best described as:

options.B: An architectural pattern in which all systems publish to and subscribe from a single structured, current-state data hub
options.E: A naming standard for tags only

questions.rationale: A pattern, not a product. Any vendor claiming to sell you a UNS is selling a component of one.

questions.question: The architectural shift a UNS represents is from:

options.B: Point-to-point integrations between every pair of systems, to hub-and-spoke publish and subscribe

questions.rationale: Point-to-point connections grow as the square of the system count. Hub-and-spoke grows linearly, which is the entire argument.

questions.question: With 6 systems each needing to exchange data with every other system, how many point-to-point integrations are required? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: Six systems give 6 times 5 divided by 2, which is 15 integrations. With a hub, each system needs one connection - six in total.

questions.question: MQTT is commonly used as the UNS transport because it:

options.B: Uses a lightweight publish and subscribe model with a central broker, well suited to many producers and consumers

questions.rationale: Publish and subscribe through a broker is exactly the hub-and-spoke pattern a UNS needs. It is not deterministic and is not used for control.

questions.question: Sparkplug B adds what to plain MQTT?

options.B: A defined topic structure, payload format and session state management including birth and death certificates

questions.rationale: Structure and state management. Plain MQTT defines transport only, leaving every implementer to invent their own conventions.

questions.question: A birth certificate in Sparkplug is published when:

options.B: A node or device comes online, declaring the full set of metrics it will publish

questions.rationale: It declares what the node offers. A subscriber can then discover the data model without being handed a spreadsheet.

questions.question: A death certificate in Sparkplug is delivered by:

options.B: The broker, using the MQTT Last Will and Testament registered when the client connected

questions.rationale: Last Will and Testament. The broker publishes it when the client disappears, which is how subscribers learn that data has gone stale.

questions.question: Why does the death certificate mechanism matter to a data consumer?

options.B: Without it, a consumer cannot distinguish a value that is genuinely steady from one whose source has disconnected

questions.rationale: A steady value and a dead source look identical unless the system tells you otherwise. This is the same problem as quality codes on a historian.

questions.question: Report by exception in a UNS means data is published:

options.B: Only when it changes beyond a defined threshold

questions.rationale: Change-driven publishing. It is what keeps the traffic manageable when thousands of tags are involved.

questions.question: A retained message on a topic provides:

options.B: The current state to any subscriber that connects later, without waiting for the next change

questions.rationale: A new subscriber gets the current value immediately. Without retained messages a subscriber sees nothing until the value happens to change.

questions.question: The topic hierarchy in a UNS is conventionally structured on:

options.B: The ISA-95 physical model - enterprise, site, area, line, cell

questions.rationale: ISA-95 gives a hierarchy the whole business already recognises. This is where Category 7 and Category 10 meet directly.

questions.question: A brownfield-first approach to UNS implementation means:

options.B: Building the UNS alongside the existing systems, so nothing is ripped out and value is delivered incrementally

questions.rationale: Alongside, not instead of. This is the framing that makes a UNS proposal acceptable to a client with a large installed base.

questions.question: Which statement about a UNS and control is correct?

options.A: A UNS replaces the control network
options.B: A UNS carries information for consumption above the control layer and is not used to close control loops

questions.rationale: It is an information architecture. Nothing in it should be in the control or safety path.

questions.question: MQTT over TLS conventionally uses which TCP port?
questions.rationale: 8883 for TLS; 1883 for plain MQTT. Worth knowing precisely when writing a firewall rule with a client's IT department.

questions.question: When proposing a UNS to a client with an installed base of several vendors' systems, the strongest argument is that it:

options.B: Removes the need to build and maintain a separate integration for every new pair of systems, so each additional consumer costs far less

questions.rationale: The economics of adding the next consumer is the argument. It is also verifiable, which makes it more persuasive than an appeal to modernity.

questions.question: In IEC 62443, a zone is:

options.B: A grouping of assets that share common security requirements

questions.rationale: A grouping by common security requirement. It often maps to a subnet but the defining property is the requirement, not the addressing.

questions.question: In IEC 62443, a conduit is:

options.B: A grouping of the communications permitted between zones, with its own security requirements

questions.rationale: The permitted communication path between zones, treated as a controlled object in its own right.

questions.question: Which IEC 62443 part covers the asset owner's cyber security management system?
questions.rationale: 62443-2-1 is the asset owner's CSMS. 3-2 is risk assessment and zone design, 3-3 is system requirements, 4-1 and 4-2 are supplier and component requirements.

questions.question: Which part covers security risk assessment and system design, including zone and conduit definition?
questions.rationale: 62443-3-2 covers the risk assessment and the partitioning into zones and conduits. It is the part most directly relevant to our design work.

questions.question: How many foundational requirements are defined in IEC 62443? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: Seven: identification and authentication control, use control, system integrity, data confidentiality, restricted data flow, timely response to events, and resource availability.

questions.question: Security Level 2 in IEC 62443 protects against:

options.B: Intentional violation using simple means with low resources, generic skills and low motivation

questions.rationale: SL2 addresses a deliberate but unsophisticated attacker. SL1 covers only casual or accidental violation.

questions.question: Security Level 3 in IEC 62443 protects against an attacker with:

options.B: Generic IT skills and low motivation
options.C: Sophisticated means, moderate resources, IACS-specific skills and moderate motivation

questions.rationale: SL3 assumes an attacker who understands control systems specifically. That distinction between generic IT skill and IACS-specific skill is what separates SL2 from SL3.

questions.question: SL-T, SL-A and SL-C respectively mean:

options.B: Target, Achieved and Capability security levels

questions.rationale: Target is what you require, Achieved is what the design delivers, Capability is what a product is able to support. Confusing them is a common error in specifications.

questions.question: A product certified to SL-C 3 means:

options.A: Any system using it is SL3
options.B: The product is capable of supporting SL3 requirements; the achieved level depends on how it is deployed and configured
options.D: It is the highest level available
options.E: It cannot be used below SL3

questions.rationale: Capability, not achievement. This mirrors exactly the SIL device certificate point in Category 8.

questions.question: The three roles defined in the IEC 62443 series are:

options.B: Asset owner, product supplier and system integrator

questions.rationale: Asset owner, product supplier, system integrator. Microverse acts as system integrator and, for MICROSYS, as product supplier - two different sets of obligations.

questions.question: The Purdue model is useful for zone definition but breaks down when applied to:

options.B: Wireless devices, cloud connections, remote access and IIoT devices that do not fit its strict hierarchy

questions.rationale: Anything that crosses levels directly defeats a strictly hierarchical model. Recognising where the model stops helping is a mark of understanding it.

questions.question: Select all criteria that would justify placing assets in separate zones.

options.B: Different operational availability requirements
options.D: Different physical colour of the cabinets

questions.rationale: Consequence, availability, ownership and regulatory obligation. Physical appearance is irrelevant.

questions.question: A safety instrumented system should normally be:

options.A: In the same zone as the BPCS for convenience
options.B: In its own zone, with a tightly defined conduit to the BPCS if any communication is required at all

questions.rationale: Its own zone, minimal conduit. This is the cyber security expression of the same independence principle that governs it functionally.

questions.question: Why is IEC 62443 relevant to a system integrator such as Microverse rather than only to the asset owner?

options.A: It is not relevant to us
options.B: 62443-2-4 places requirements on service providers, and clients increasingly ask integrators to demonstrate their own security practices

questions.rationale: Integrator obligations are explicit in the series, and clients are starting to ask. Being unable to answer is becoming a commercial disadvantage.

questions.question: A peer-reviewed criticism of IEC 62443 is that:

options.B: The series does not use a single consistent definition of zone across all its parts, which can create ambiguity in application

questions.rationale: The definition is not perfectly consistent across parts. Knowing where a standard is genuinely ambiguous, rather than assuming you misread it, is a mark of expertise.

questions.question: Every conduit in a segmentation design should be documented with:

options.B: Source, destination, protocol, port, direction and the controls applied

questions.rationale: Six attributes minimum. An undocumented flow is an uncontrolled flow, and it will be found in an audit.

questions.question: In practice, the minimum security level normally targeted for OT zones is:

options.B: SL 1

questions.rationale: SL2 is the practical minimum for most OT zones. It is a number worth quoting in a proposal because it anchors the discussion.

questions.question: The industrial DMZ exists so that:

options.B: No direct routable path exists between IT and OT, with traffic brokered by servers in the DMZ
options.D: OT systems can be patched automatically

questions.rationale: Brokering rather than routing. A system in the DMZ terminates the IT connection and a separate connection serves OT.

questions.question: A data diode provides:

options.B: Physically enforced one-way data flow, so no traffic can return from the receiving side

questions.rationale: One-way flow enforced by physics rather than configuration. It is used where the consequence of an inbound path is unacceptable.

questions.question: The main operational limitation of a data diode is that:

options.B: Nothing can come back, so protocols requiring acknowledgement or bidirectional handshake will not work across it

questions.rationale: No return path means no acknowledgement. Applications must be designed for one-way transfer, which rules out most standard protocols.

questions.question: Select all controls that legitimately belong on an IT to OT conduit.

options.A: A firewall with an explicit allow list of source, destination, protocol and port
options.B: A broker or proxy in the DMZ that terminates both connections
options.C: Logging and monitoring of the traffic crossing the boundary
options.D: Allowing any protocol provided the source is trusted

questions.rationale: Explicit allow lists, brokering, logging and authentication. Trusting a source and allowing any protocol from it defeats the boundary.

questions.question: Defence in depth means:

options.B: Multiple independent layers of control, so the compromise of one does not expose everything behind it

questions.rationale: Independent layers. It is the same logic as layers of protection in process safety, applied to security.

questions.question: Secure remote access for our AMC work should be designed as:

options.A: A permanent open VPN to the control network
options.B: Time-limited, authenticated, monitored access brokered through the DMZ, initiated and approved by the client
options.D: Shared credentials for the service team

questions.rationale: Brokered, time-limited, authenticated and approved. A permanent open path to a client's control network is a liability we should not want.

questions.question: Shared service account credentials for a support team are a problem because:

options.B: Actions cannot be attributed to an individual, and revoking access when someone leaves is impractical

questions.rationale: No attribution and no clean revocation. Both matter after an incident and both are asked about in an audit.

questions.question: An engineering workstation used for both OT configuration and general office work represents:

options.B: A bridge across the segmentation boundary that defeats the design regardless of the firewall rules

questions.rationale: A dual-purpose machine is a routable path in human form. Dedicated OT machines are a basic and frequently ignored control.

questions.question: Removable media controls in an OT environment exist because:

options.B: USB devices bypass every network control and have been the initial vector in significant OT incidents

questions.rationale: A USB stick crosses every firewall you have. Stuxnet is the canonical example, and the control is still routinely absent.

questions.question: When a client's IT department demands the control network be brought onto the corporate domain, the technically correct response is:

options.B: Explain that domain membership creates a direct dependency and a routable path across the boundary, and propose a segmented design that meets their management objectives differently

questions.rationale: Address the objective, not the proposal. IT usually wants manageability, which can be achieved without dissolving the boundary.

questions.question: Network monitoring in an OT zone should preferentially use:

options.B: Passive monitoring via port mirroring, since active scanning can disrupt legacy control devices

questions.rationale: Passive first. Active scans have been known to crash legacy PLCs, which turns a security measure into a production incident.

questions.question: An asset inventory is described as the foundation of OT security because:

options.B: You cannot protect, patch or segment what you do not know exists

questions.rationale: Everything else depends on knowing what is there. Most plants discover devices they did not know about the first time they do this properly.

questions.question: When we deliver a system, the security-relevant handover documentation should include:

options.A: The password list in plain text
options.B: The zone and conduit design, the allow lists applied, accounts created and their purpose, and the hardening steps performed

questions.rationale: Documented and handed over properly. Withholding it does not improve security; it just means the client cannot maintain what we built.

questions.question: Structuring MQTT topics on the ISA-95 physical model gives:

options.B: A hierarchy that both plant and business staff already recognise, so subscriptions can be made by area or line without a lookup table

questions.rationale: A shared, meaningful hierarchy. Subscribing to everything in one area becomes a single wildcard rather than a list of tags.
questions.moduleTopic: Mapping ISA-95 onto a topic hierarchy

questions.question: A topic path such as enterprise/site/area/line/cell/metric reflects:

options.B: The ISA-95 physical hierarchy applied to the namespace

questions.rationale: It is the ISA-95 physical model expressed as a path. That is the standard convention and it should not be invented afresh per project.
questions.moduleTopic: Mapping ISA-95 onto a topic hierarchy

questions.question: A wildcard subscription to one area's topic branch allows a consumer to:

options.B: Receive everything published within that area without knowing the individual tag names in advance

questions.rationale: Discovery by structure rather than by list. This is the practical payoff of a disciplined hierarchy.
questions.moduleTopic: Mapping ISA-95 onto a topic hierarchy

questions.question: Select all elements that a data contract for a UNS should define.

options.A: Naming rules for topics and metrics
options.B: Payload schema and data types
options.C: Units of measure and their convention
options.D: A timestamp convention and its source

questions.rationale: Naming, schema, units and timestamps. Cable routing is a different document entirely.
questions.moduleTopic: Mapping ISA-95 onto a topic hierarchy

questions.question: Why must the timestamp convention be defined in the data contract?

options.B: Because a mixture of source time, broker time and local time zones makes correlation across systems impossible

questions.rationale: Mixed time bases silently corrupt every correlation. Defining source time in UTC is the usual answer, and it must be a decision rather than an accident.
questions.moduleTopic: Mapping ISA-95 onto a topic hierarchy

questions.question: Quality should be carried in the UNS payload because:

options.B: A consumer must be able to distinguish a real value from a stale or failed one, exactly as with a historian

questions.rationale: Same principle as the historian quality code. A value without quality is a number a consumer must trust blindly.
questions.moduleTopic: Mapping ISA-95 onto a topic hierarchy

questions.question: Publishing the same metric under two different topic paths in a UNS is:

options.B: A problem, because consumers cannot tell which is authoritative and the two will diverge

questions.rationale: Two paths to the same fact will eventually disagree. One authoritative publisher per metric is a core rule.
questions.moduleTopic: Mapping ISA-95 onto a topic hierarchy

questions.question: Ownership of each topic branch should be:

options.B: Assigned to one publishing system, so responsibility for correctness is unambiguous

questions.rationale: One owner per branch. Ambiguous ownership is the source of most data disputes.
questions.moduleTopic: Mapping ISA-95 onto a topic hierarchy

questions.question: Renaming topics after consumers are connected is problematic because:

options.B: Every subscriber breaks, which is why the hierarchy should be designed with care before consumers are built

questions.rationale: The namespace is an interface. Changing it breaks everything downstream, so it deserves the same care as any published interface.
questions.moduleTopic: Mapping ISA-95 onto a topic hierarchy

questions.question: A UNS design that mirrors the plant hierarchy rather than the control system architecture is preferred because:

options.B: The plant hierarchy is stable and meaningful to the business, while the control architecture changes when equipment is replaced

questions.rationale: Plant structure outlives control hardware. Building the namespace on the controller layout means rebuilding it at every upgrade.
questions.moduleTopic: Mapping ISA-95 onto a topic hierarchy

questions.question: Where a UNS spans several sites, the top of the hierarchy should be:

options.B: The enterprise and site, so data from each site is unambiguously identified

questions.rationale: Enterprise and site at the top, exactly as ISA-95 defines. This is what makes multi-site aggregation possible.
questions.moduleTopic: Mapping ISA-95 onto a topic hierarchy

questions.question: A client asks for tag names in the UNS identical to their DCS tag numbers. The considered response is:

options.B: Explain that DCS tags carry no hierarchy or business meaning, and propose the ISA-95 structure with the DCS tag retained as metadata

questions.rationale: Keep the DCS tag as metadata, not as the structure. Both needs are met and neither is compromised.
questions.moduleTopic: Mapping ISA-95 onto a topic hierarchy

questions.question: The connection between Category 7 and Category 10 in our programme is that:

options.B: ISA-95 defines the hierarchy that both the documentation set and the data namespace are built on

questions.rationale: One model, two applications. Teaching them separately without making the connection wastes half the value of both.
questions.moduleTopic: Mapping ISA-95 onto a topic hierarchy

questions.question: Sparkplug metric names within a topic should be:

options.B: Governed by the naming rules in the data contract, so the same physical quantity is named identically everywhere

questions.rationale: Consistent naming is what allows a consumer to write one piece of logic that works across every line. Free-form naming forces per-device special cases.
questions.moduleTopic: Mapping ISA-95 onto a topic hierarchy

questions.question: When designing the namespace for a client with an existing ISA-95 aligned MES, we should:

options.B: Align to their existing hierarchy, since a second incompatible model creates permanent translation work

questions.rationale: Align to what exists. Two incompatible hierarchies mean a mapping layer that must be maintained forever.
questions.moduleTopic: Mapping ISA-95 onto a topic hierarchy

questions.question: The most commonly cited reason UNS projects fail is that the failures are:

options.B: Organisational - no agreed ownership, naming discipline or data contracts

questions.rationale: Organisational rather than technical. The broker is rarely the problem; agreement about what publishes what usually is.
questions.moduleTopic: What makes a UNS survive contact with a plant

questions.question: A data contract in a UNS is:

options.B: The agreed technical definition of naming, payload structure, units, timestamps and quality that all publishers must follow

questions.rationale: A technical agreement between publishers and consumers. Without it every publisher invents its own conventions and consumers write per-source special cases.
questions.moduleTopic: What makes a UNS survive contact with a plant

questions.question: Select all measures that improve the resilience of a UNS in production.

options.A: Retained messages carrying current state for each topic
options.B: Last Will and Testament configured for every client
options.C: Health and status topics published by each node
options.D: Fit-for-purpose QoS chosen per topic rather than maximum everywhere
options.E: Allowing each publisher to choose its own naming

questions.rationale: Retained state, LWT, health topics and appropriate QoS. Free naming is the thing that undermines all of it.
questions.moduleTopic: What makes a UNS survive contact with a plant

questions.question: Setting QoS 2 on every topic is poor practice because:

options.B: It imposes the highest overhead everywhere, when most process values are better served by lower QoS with report by exception

questions.rationale: Fit for purpose per topic. A value republished every few seconds does not need exactly-once delivery guarantees.
questions.moduleTopic: What makes a UNS survive contact with a plant

questions.question: A health or heartbeat topic published by each node allows consumers to:

options.B: Distinguish a healthy source publishing steady values from one that has silently stopped

questions.rationale: It answers the steady-versus-dead question explicitly rather than by inference. Same problem as quality codes, solved a different way.
questions.moduleTopic: What makes a UNS survive contact with a plant

questions.question: The broker in a UNS should be treated as:

options.B: A critical shared infrastructure component requiring redundancy, monitoring and change control

questions.rationale: Everything depends on it, so it needs the treatment given to shared infrastructure. An unmonitored single broker is a single point of failure for the whole data architecture.
questions.moduleTopic: What makes a UNS survive contact with a plant

questions.question: Access control on a UNS broker should be applied so that:

options.A: Every client can publish and subscribe to everything
options.B: Each client can publish only to the topics it owns and subscribe only to what it needs
options.C: Only the broker administrator has access
options.D: Access is by IP address alone
options.E: No controls are needed inside the plant

questions.rationale: Least privilege by topic. Unrestricted publish rights mean any compromised client can inject values anywhere in the namespace.
questions.moduleTopic: What makes a UNS survive contact with a plant

questions.question: Where should an edge gateway that bridges the control layer into the UNS normally sit?

options.B: At the boundary, publishing outward, with the conduit and its controls documented in the segmentation design

questions.rationale: At a documented boundary. A gateway that quietly bridges two zones without appearing in the conduit list is exactly what an audit will find.
questions.moduleTopic: What makes a UNS survive contact with a plant

questions.question: A UNS design that ignores IEC 62443 segmentation is likely to:

options.B: Fail the client's own security review, even if it works technically

questions.rationale: It will work and it will not be approved. Designing the data architecture and the segmentation together avoids a late and expensive redesign.
questions.moduleTopic: What makes a UNS survive contact with a plant

questions.question: A phased UNS rollout is preferred over a single large implementation because:

options.B: Early phases deliver visible value and expose naming and ownership problems while they are still cheap to correct
options.E: It avoids the need for data contracts

questions.rationale: Early value and early error discovery. Naming mistakes found in phase one cost days; found in phase five they cost a redesign.
questions.moduleTopic: What makes a UNS survive contact with a plant

questions.question: Before the first topic is published, the artefacts that should exist are:

options.B: The namespace design, the data contract, and the agreed ownership of each branch

questions.rationale: Design, contract and ownership. Publishing before these exist guarantees a namespace that has to be rebuilt.
questions.moduleTopic: What makes a UNS survive contact with a plant

questions.question: For Microverse, the honest scope boundary on a UNS project today is:

options.B: Publishing our own systems correctly into a namespace, with the enterprise-wide architecture and governance owned or explicitly contracted with the client

questions.rationale: Be clear about what we own. Taking responsibility for enterprise governance we cannot enforce is a commitment we would fail to meet.
questions.moduleTopic: What makes a UNS survive contact with a plant

questions.question: A client proposes that their ERP writes setpoints directly into the control system through the UNS. Our position should be:

options.A: Agree, it is a supported pattern
options.B: Explain that command paths from business systems into control require a separate, deliberately designed and secured mechanism, not the information namespace

questions.rationale: Information flow and command flow are different problems. Conflating them puts a business system in the control path.
questions.moduleTopic: What makes a UNS survive contact with a plant

questions.question: The measure that best demonstrates a UNS is delivering value is:

options.B: The reduction in effort and time to connect each additional consumer, compared with the previous point-to-point approach

questions.rationale: Marginal cost of the next integration is the whole argument for the architecture, so it is the right thing to measure.
questions.moduleTopic: What makes a UNS survive contact with a plant

questions.question: The single most valuable internal document for our own UNS and cloud work would be:

options.B: A documented Miralys and Aletix reference architecture covering edge placement, conduit rules and secure remote access

questions.rationale: A reference architecture is reusable on every project, answers the client IT department's questions in advance, and stops the knowledge sitting in two people's heads.
questions.moduleTopic: What makes a UNS survive contact with a plant

questions.question: In a cane sugar factory, the purpose of the milling tandem is to:

options.B: Extract juice from prepared cane by crushing it through successive mills

questions.rationale: Juice extraction. Preparation by knives and shredder comes first; clarification, evaporation and crystallisation come later.

questions.question: Imbibition water is added at the milling stage to:

options.B: Improve extraction by diluting the residual juice in the bagasse before the next mill

questions.rationale: It dilutes the juice remaining in the fibre so more sucrose is recovered downstream. More imbibition means better extraction but more water to evaporate later.

questions.question: Bagasse leaving the mills is normally used as:

options.B: Fuel for the boilers, supporting the factory's own steam and power generation

questions.rationale: Bagasse fires the boilers. That is why almost every sugar factory has a captive power plant attached, and why Categories 9 and 3 overlap on these jobs.

questions.question: Brix is a measure of:

options.B: Total dissolved solids in the juice

questions.rationale: Brix is total dissolved solids. Pol measures sucrose specifically, and purity is the ratio between them.

questions.question: A juice sample has a Pol of 78 and a Brix of 85. What is its purity, expressed as a percentage? Enter a number to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: Purity is Pol divided by Brix, times 100 - 78 divided by 85 gives 91.8 percent. Purity is the key indicator of juice quality through the process.

questions.question: Clarification of raw juice by liming and sulphitation is done to:

options.B: Precipitate impurities so they can be removed in the clarifier

questions.rationale: It removes non-sugar impurities. The mud is then filtered and the clear juice goes to evaporation.

questions.question: The multiple effect evaporator is used to:

options.B: Concentrate clear juice into syrup by removing water, reusing vapour from each effect to heat the next

questions.rationale: Water removal with vapour reuse. The multiple effect arrangement exists to cut steam consumption, which is why its control affects the whole factory's energy balance.

questions.question: Pan boiling is carried out under vacuum because:

options.B: Vacuum lowers the boiling point, preventing sucrose degradation and colour formation at high temperature
options.C: It improves the vacuum pump efficiency
options.E: It removes the need for seeding

questions.rationale: Lower boiling point protects the sucrose. Sugar degrades and darkens if boiled at atmospheric temperature.

questions.question: Final molasses leaving the sugar house is:

options.B: The exhausted syrup from which no further sugar can economically be crystallised, commonly sold or fermented to ethanol

questions.rationale: It is the link between our sugar clients and our ethanol clients. The same group often runs both plants on one site.

questions.question: In a molasses-based distillery, molasses is first:

options.B: Diluted with water to a suitable sugar concentration before fermentation

questions.rationale: Dilution to a fermentable sugar concentration. Yeast cannot work at the osmotic pressure of undiluted molasses.

questions.question: Fermentation converts sugars into:

options.B: Ethanol and oxygen

questions.rationale: Ethanol and CO2, with heat released. The heat is why fermenters need cooling to hold temperature.

questions.question: Fermentation temperature is controlled because:

options.B: Yeast activity falls sharply outside a fairly narrow range, and excessive temperature kills the yeast

questions.rationale: Yeast has a narrow optimum, typically around 30 to 32 degC. Losing temperature control loses the batch.

questions.question: The fermented liquid sent to distillation is called:

options.B: Wash or beer, typically containing around 8 to 10 percent alcohol by volume

questions.rationale: Wash or beer. Spent wash is what remains after distillation removes the alcohol.

questions.question: Rectified spirit from a conventional distillation column reaches approximately:

options.B: 95 to 96 percent alcohol by volume

questions.rationale: About 95 to 96 percent, which is the ethanol-water azeotrope. Ordinary distillation cannot go beyond it.

questions.question: To produce anhydrous fuel ethanol above the azeotrope, the process used is:

options.B: Dehydration, commonly by molecular sieve pressure swing adsorption

questions.rationale: Molecular sieve dehydration is the standard route. Simply distilling harder cannot pass the azeotrope.

questions.question: Spent wash from a distillery is significant because it:

options.B: Has a very high organic load and requires substantial treatment, commonly biomethanation and concentration or incineration

questions.rationale: Very high COD makes it one of the hardest effluents in our client base, and it is why distillery jobs almost always include an effluent scope.

questions.question: Continuous fermentation differs from batch fermentation in that continuous:

options.B: Runs steadily with continuous feed and draw-off, giving higher throughput but demanding tighter control and contamination management

questions.rationale: Higher throughput, tighter control, greater contamination risk. The control philosophy differs substantially from batch.

questions.question: Carbon dioxide released during fermentation is a concern because it:

options.B: Is an asphyxiation hazard in enclosed areas and must be vented and, where required, monitored

questions.rationale: It is heavier than air and displaces oxygen. Fermenter houses need ventilation and, on many plants, gas detection.

questions.question: The preliminary stage of effluent treatment removes:

options.B: Large solids and grit by screening and grit removal

questions.rationale: Screening and grit removal protect the downstream equipment. Skipping it damages pumps and blocks diffusers.

questions.question: An equalisation tank is provided to:

options.B: Even out variations in flow and load so downstream stages see steady conditions

questions.rationale: Buffering flow and load. Biological treatment performs badly when the load swings, so the equalisation tank protects it.

questions.question: Primary treatment principally removes:

options.B: Settleable and floating solids, typically in a primary clarifier

questions.rationale: Physical separation of settleable solids. Dissolved organics are removed biologically in secondary treatment.

questions.question: Secondary treatment is primarily:

options.B: A biological process in which microorganisms consume dissolved organic matter

questions.rationale: Biological. Aeration tanks, MBBR and UASB are all variants of using organisms to consume the organic load.

questions.question: BOD is a measure of:

options.B: The oxygen demand exerted by biodegradable organic matter

questions.rationale: Biochemical oxygen demand indicates the biodegradable organic load. COD is the broader chemical oxygen demand, which includes non-biodegradable matter.

questions.question: Which stage of a typical ETP consumes the most electrical energy?

options.B: Aeration in the biological stage

questions.rationale: Aeration dominates the energy bill, often by a wide margin. That is why dissolved oxygen control is where the savings are.

questions.question: Tertiary treatment is applied to:

options.B: Polish the effluent further, for example by filtration, activated carbon, membranes or disinfection, to meet discharge or reuse limits

questions.rationale: Final polishing to meet a discharge or reuse standard. Whether it is needed depends entirely on the consent limits.

questions.question: Sludge handling exists to:

options.B: Thicken and dewater the solids produced by the process so they can be disposed of or reused

questions.rationale: Volume reduction and dewatering. The sludge line is often neglected in design and is a frequent source of operating problems.

questions.question: A UASB reactor differs from an activated sludge aeration tank in that a UASB is:

options.B: Anaerobic, requiring no aeration and producing biogas

questions.rationale: Anaerobic with biogas as a byproduct. It suits high-strength effluents such as distillery spent wash, where aerobic treatment would be prohibitively energy intensive.

questions.question: Dissolved oxygen in an aeration tank is typically controlled to around:

options.B: 2 mg per litre

questions.rationale: Around 2 mg per litre is the usual target. Below that the biology suffers; well above it, energy is being wasted on blowers.

questions.question: Controlling dissolved oxygen rather than running blowers at a fixed speed saves energy because:

options.B: Air demand varies with the incoming organic load, so fixed-speed operation over-aerates most of the time
options.E: It removes the need for a clarifier

questions.rationale: Load varies through the day. Matching air supply to actual demand is the single largest energy saving available on most ETPs.

questions.question: A diffused aeration system delivers air through:

options.B: Diffusers at the tank floor fed by blowers, producing fine bubbles that transfer oxygen as they rise
options.D: A venturi in the inlet pipe

questions.rationale: Floor diffusers fed by blowers. Blocked or fouled diffusers raise the blower pressure and quietly destroy the transfer efficiency.

questions.question: MLSS in an activated sludge process refers to:

options.B: Mixed liquor suspended solids, the concentration of biomass in the aeration tank

questions.rationale: The biomass concentration. Together with the incoming load it determines the food to microorganism ratio the process is running at.

questions.question: An equalisation tank has a working volume of 500 cubic metres and receives a steady flow of 100 cubic metres per hour. What is the hydraulic retention time, in hours? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: Volume divided by flow - 500 divided by 100 equals 5 hours. HRT is the basic sizing parameter for every tank in an ETP.

questions.question: A secondary clarifier following an aeration tank is used to:

options.B: Separate the biomass from the treated water, returning some as return activated sludge and wasting the surplus

questions.rationale: Separation and sludge return. The return activated sludge stream is what maintains the biomass inventory in the aeration tank.

questions.question: pH correction is applied in an ETP because:

options.B: Biological treatment and many chemical processes only work within a limited pH range, and discharge consents specify limits

questions.rationale: Biology has a narrow pH tolerance and the discharge consent will specify a range. pH control is one of the most common loops on an ETP.

questions.question: A pH neutralisation loop is difficult to control because:

options.B: The relationship between reagent added and pH is strongly non-linear, with very high gain near neutrality

questions.rationale: The titration curve is extremely steep around pH 7. A loop tuned for the flat region oscillates violently near neutrality, which is why staged tanks and gain scheduling are common.

questions.question: Coagulation and flocculation are used to:

options.B: Destabilise and agglomerate fine suspended particles so they settle

questions.rationale: Fine particles that would never settle alone are bound into larger flocs. Dosing control here directly affects clarifier performance.

questions.question: Swell in a boiler drum refers to:

options.B: An apparent rise in level caused by steam bubbles expanding when drum pressure falls

questions.rationale: Bubbles expand as pressure drops, so the indicated level rises even though the water mass is falling. It is the central problem in drum level control.
questions.moduleTopic: Drum level: why one element is not enough

questions.question: On a sudden increase in steam demand, drum level initially:

options.A: Falls, because water is being consumed
options.B: Rises, because falling pressure expands the steam bubbles below the surface

questions.rationale: It rises - the opposite of what the mass balance would suggest. That is precisely why single element control fails on swinging load.
questions.moduleTopic: Drum level: why one element is not enough

questions.question: Shrink occurs when:

options.B: Load decreases and rising drum pressure collapses the steam bubbles, so indicated level falls

questions.rationale: Rising pressure collapses the bubbles and the level drops even though mass is being added. Shrink and swell are the same phenomenon in opposite directions.
questions.moduleTopic: Drum level: why one element is not enough

questions.question: With single element control, a swell event causes the controller to:

options.B: Reduce feedwater at exactly the moment more water is actually needed

questions.rationale: It acts on the false high level and starves the boiler. The error is not a tuning problem - the controller is being told the wrong thing.
questions.moduleTopic: Drum level: why one element is not enough

questions.question: Single element drum level control is acceptable when:

options.B: Load is steady and the boiler is small, so swell and shrink effects are minor

questions.rationale: Steady load on a small boiler. It is not wrong in every case, and specifying three element on a small steady package boiler is over-engineering.
questions.moduleTopic: Drum level: why one element is not enough

questions.question: Why is drum level a critical measurement rather than merely an operational one?

options.B: Low level uncovers the tubes and risks overheating and failure; high level carries water into the steam and can damage the turbine

questions.rationale: Both extremes damage equipment, which is why drum level trips exist and why the measurement is usually redundant.
questions.moduleTopic: Drum level: why one element is not enough

questions.question: Drum level measured by differential pressure requires compensation for:

options.B: Drum pressure, because the density of both water and steam changes strongly with it

questions.rationale: Uncompensated DP level is only correct at the calibration pressure. Pressure compensation is standard on boiler drum level.
questions.moduleTopic: Drum level: why one element is not enough

questions.question: The correct first response to a report that drum level control is unstable is to:

options.B: Establish whether the instability is swell and shrink from load swings, a measurement compensation error, or a genuine tuning problem

questions.rationale: Diagnose before tuning. The three causes need three different remedies and only one of them is tuning.
questions.moduleTopic: Drum level: why one element is not enough

questions.question: Select all statements that are true about swell and shrink.

options.A: They are caused by steam bubbles changing volume with pressure
options.B: They make the level move opposite to the mass balance for a short period
options.C: They are worse on boilers with rapidly changing load
options.D: They can be eliminated by retuning the level controller
options.E: They are the reason feedforward from steam flow is used

questions.rationale: Physical phenomena that tuning cannot remove. The remedy is a control structure that anticipates load, not a different set of constants.
questions.moduleTopic: Drum level: why one element is not enough

questions.question: A boiler serving a batch process with sudden large steam draws needs:

options.B: Three element control, because load swings are exactly the condition single element cannot handle

questions.rationale: Sudden large load changes are the worst case for swell and shrink, so the feedforward from steam flow is essential.
questions.moduleTopic: Drum level: why one element is not enough

questions.question: Drum level is described as an integrating process because:

options.B: Any imbalance between feedwater and steam flow causes the level to keep changing rather than settling at a new value

questions.rationale: It does not self-regulate. This changes both the tuning approach and the reason feedforward is so effective here.
questions.moduleTopic: Drum level: why one element is not enough

questions.question: Excessive integral action on a drum level controller typically produces:

options.B: Overshoot and cycling, because the controller keeps acting on an integrating process that will eventually respond

questions.rationale: Integrating processes need much less integral action than self-regulating ones. Over-integrating is the most common drum level tuning error.
questions.moduleTopic: Drum level: why one element is not enough

questions.question: Two independent drum level transmitters with a deviation alarm are provided because:

options.B: A single failed level measurement can lead to tube damage or turbine water carryover, and the deviation alarm reveals a drifting channel before the trip is compromised

questions.rationale: The consequences of a wrong level are severe. Redundancy plus deviation monitoring is standard, and the trip function is normally separate again.
questions.moduleTopic: Drum level: why one element is not enough

questions.question: The drum level trip function should be:

options.A: The same measurement used for control
options.B: Independent of the control measurement, in line with the BPCS and SIS separation principle
options.D: Set by the operator each shift

questions.rationale: Independent measurement for the trip. This is Category 8's independence principle applied to the most common boiler protection function.
questions.moduleTopic: Drum level: why one element is not enough

questions.question: A boiler with a persistent low drum level alarm at high load, with the feedwater valve fully open, indicates:

options.B: A capacity limitation - the feedwater pump, valve or supply pressure cannot meet demand

questions.rationale: A saturated output is a capacity problem, not a control problem. No amount of tuning creates flow that is not available.
questions.moduleTopic: Drum level: why one element is not enough

questions.question: The three elements in three element drum level control are:

options.B: Drum level, steam flow and feedwater flow
options.C: Level, fuel flow and air flow
options.D: Level, drum pressure and feedwater temperature
options.E: Steam flow, fuel flow and air flow

questions.rationale: Level as the master, steam flow as the feedforward and feedwater flow as the inner cascade measurement.

questions.question: In three element control, steam flow is used as:

options.B: A feedforward signal that anticipates the required feedwater flow before the level moves

questions.rationale: Feedforward. It acts on the disturbance before the level responds, which is what defeats the swell and shrink problem.

questions.question: In three element control, feedwater flow forms:

options.B: The inner cascade loop, whose setpoint comes from the level controller and the feedforward

questions.rationale: The inner flow loop. It rejects feedwater pressure and valve non-linearity before they reach the drum.

questions.question: Which disturbance does the inner feedwater flow loop specifically reject?

options.B: Feedwater header pressure variation and control valve non-linearity

questions.rationale: It catches supply-side disturbances locally. Without it, a header pressure change moves the flow and the level controller only notices later.

questions.question: The level controller's output in a three element scheme is:

options.B: A feedwater flow setpoint, which is then trimmed or summed with the steam flow feedforward

questions.rationale: It sets a flow, not a valve position. That is what makes it a cascade rather than direct control.

questions.question: The correct commissioning sequence for a three element scheme is:

options.B: Tune the feedwater flow loop first and leave it in auto, then close and tune the level loop, then commission the feedforward

questions.rationale: Inner loop first, then outer, then feedforward. Tuning the level loop against an untuned flow loop means doing it twice.

questions.question: During startup at very low load, three element control is often switched to single element because:

options.B: Steam and feedwater flow measurements are inaccurate at very low flow, so the feedforward and inner loop signals are unreliable

questions.rationale: DP flow measurement is poor at low flow. Switching schemes with load is standard, and the transfer must be bumpless.

questions.question: The transfer between single and three element control must be:

options.B: Bumpless, with the inner loop setpoint initialised so the feedwater flow does not step

questions.rationale: A step in feedwater flow at the changeover disturbs the drum at exactly the point in startup where level is most sensitive.

questions.question: Select all reasons the inner feedwater flow loop improves drum level control.

options.A: It rejects feedwater header pressure disturbances locally
options.B: It linearises the effect of the control valve as seen by the level loop
options.C: It allows the feedforward signal to be applied in flow units
options.D: It removes the need for level measurement
options.E: It compensates for drum pressure changes

questions.rationale: Disturbance rejection, linearisation and a common unit for the feedforward. It does not replace the level measurement or compensate drum pressure.

questions.question: Feedwater flow measurement for a three element scheme should be taken:

options.A: Downstream of the control valve only
options.B: Where it represents the actual flow entering the drum, with attention to the effect of any recirculation or attemperator take-off

questions.rationale: It must represent the flow that actually reaches the drum. Take-offs downstream of the measurement point cause a persistent mass balance error.

questions.question: If the steam flow feedforward signal fails to zero, the scheme should:

options.B: Detect the failure and fall back to level control alone, with an alarm
